sources.body: YouTube is launching a new AI feature that creates a personalized video feed based on descriptions of what you want to watch. To access it, click on the “Your custom feed” tab at the top of the YouTube homepage and enter a prompt description into the AI text box.

extraction.body: YouTube is launching a new AI feature that creates a personalized video feed based on descriptions of what you want to watch. In its announcement, YouTube says custom content feeds can be built around your specific interests, moods, or favorite topics, which you can then pin to the top of your YouTube homepage — making it easy to jump back into the feed. This feature is currently rolling out with English language support to YouTube users in the US who are signed in on the YouTube mobile app or desktop. To access it, click on the “Your custom feed” tab at the top of the YouTube homepage and enter a prompt description into the AI text box. For example, you can ask the YouTube AI to “help me unwind with guided meditations under 10 minutes,” or for “deep-dive tech podcasts about AI,” and then receive a curated feed based on your request. It’s similar to other AI-powered feed customization features we’ve seen from other platforms, including Spotify’s prompted playlists. Instagram also gave users more control over their Reels feed algorithm in December, though that uses topic lists rather than descriptive prompts. YouTube says that prompts can be edited at any time to “generate a brand new space” by selecting the text box at the top of your custom feed. To see the “Your custom feed” tab, YouTube says you need to ensure your search and watch history are enabled in your account settings. If the AI messes up your feed request, you can also report the issue to YouTube by clicking the 3-dot menu on the feature tab and selecting “Something wrong?” to leave feedback.

extraction.body: Low-quality AI-generated content is now saturating social media – and generating about $117m a year, data shows More than 20% of the videos that YouTube’s algorithm shows to new users are “AI slop” – low-quality AI-generated content designed to farm views, research has found . The video-editing company Kapwing surveyed 15,000 of the world’s most popular YouTube channels – the top 100 in every country – and found that 278 of them contain only AI slop . Together, these AI slop channels have amassed more than 63bn views and 221 million subscribers, generating about $117m (£90m) in revenue each year, according to estimates. The researchers also made a new YouTube account and found that 104 of the first 500 videos recommended to its feed were AI slop. One-third of the 500 videos were “brainrot”, a category that includes AI slop and other low-quality content made to monetise attention. The findings are a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry that is saturating big social media platforms – from X to Meta to YouTube – and defining a new era of content: decontextualised, addictive and international. A Guardian analysis this year found that nearly 10% of YouTube’s fastest-growing channels were AI slop, racking up millions of views despite the platform’s efforts to curb “inauthentic content”. The channels found by Kapwing are globally distributed and globally watched. They have millions of subscribers: in Spain, 20 million people, or nearly half the country’s population, follow the trending AI channels. AI channels have 18 million followers in Egypt, 14.5 million in the US, and 13.5 million in Brazil. Bandar Apna Dost , the most-viewed channel in the study, is based in India and now has 2.4bn views. It features the adventures of an anthropomorphic rhesus monkey and a muscular character modelled off the Incredible Hulk who fights demons and travels on a helicopter made of tomatoes. Kapwing estimated that the channel could make as much as $4.25m. Its owner did not respond to a query from the Guardian. Rohini Lakshané, a researcher on technology and digital rights, said Bandar Apna Dost’s popularity most likely stems from its absurdity, its hyper-masculine tropes and the fact that it lacks a plot, which makes it accessible to new viewers. Pouty Frenchie , based in Singapore, has 2bn views and appears to target children. It chronicles the adventures of a French bulldog – driving to a candy forest, eating crystal sushi – many of them set to a soundtrack of children’s laughter. Kapwing estimates it makes nearly $4m a year. Cuentos Facinantes, based in the US, also appears to target children with cartoon storylines, and has 6.65 million subscribers – making it the most-subscribed channel in the study. Meanwhile, The AI World , based in Pakistan, contains AI-generated shorts of catastrophic flooding in Pakistan, with titles such as Poor People, Poor Family, and Flood Kitchen. Many of these videos are set to a soundtrack called Relaxing Rain, Thunder & Lightning Ambience for Sleep. The channel itself has 1.3bn views. It’s hard to say exactly how significant these channels are compared with the vast sea of content already on YouTube. The platform does not release information on how many views it has yearly, or how many of these are from AI content. In a comment to the Guardian, a YouTube spokesperson said they had terminated one “AI slop” channel identified in Kapwing’s study, and removed others from its monetisation programmes. But behind these uncanny scenes of candy forests and disasters is a semi-structured, growing industry of people trying to find new ways to monetise the world’s most powerful platforms using AI tools. “There are these big swathes of people on Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord and message boards exchanging tips and ideas [and] selling courses about how to sort of make slop that will be engaging enough to earn money,” said Max Read , a journalist who has written extensively on AI slop. “They have what they call niches. One that I noticed recently is AI videos of people’s pressure cookers exploding on the stove.” While creators of AI slop are everywhere, Read said that many come from English-speaking countries with relatively strong internet connectivity, where the median wage is less than the amount they can make on YouTube. “It’s mostly sort of middle-income countries like Ukraine, lots and lots of people in India, Kenya, Nigeria, a fair number in Brazil. You see Vietnam, too. Places with relative freedom online to access social media sites,” he said. It’s not always easy to be an AI slop creator. For one thing, creator programmes on YouTube and Meta aren’t always transparent about who they pay for content, and how much, said Read. For another, the AI slop ecosystem is full of scammers: people selling tips and courses on how to make viral content – who often make more money than the AI slop producers themselves. But, at least for some, it’s a living. And while new, attention-grabbing ideas – such as exploding pressure cookers – constantly emerge, when it comes to AI slop, human creativity matters far less than the algorithms that distribute the content on Meta and YouTube. “These websites are huge A/B testing machines just by their nature,” said Read. “Almost anything that you can think of, you could already find on Facebook. So the question is, how do you find the things that are kind of doing well, and then how do you scale that? How do you make 10 of them?” A YouTube spokesperson said: “Generative AI is a tool, and like any tool it can be used to make both high- and low-quality content. We remain focused on connecting our users with high-quality content, regardless of how it was made. All content uploaded to YouTube must comply with our community guidelines, and if we find that content violates a policy, we remove it.” The Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said. If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it ( iOS / Android ) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. SecureDrop, instant messengers, email, telephone and post If you can safely use the Tor network without being observed or monitored, you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via our SecureDrop platform . Finally, our guide at theguardian.com/tips lists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each. sources.title: YouTube will let you build your own algorithm with AI
passages: YouTube says it’s going to let you build your own algorithm — well, kind of.
The company on Wednesday announced a new feature called custom feeds that allows you to describe, in your own words, the kinds of videos you’d like YouTube to recommend to you.

To create one, you type a description of what you want the feed to be about into a prompt box on YouTube, whether that’s a feed dedicated to a particular interest or one that serves some other purpose.
The new feeds, however, will not replace YouTube’s main feed, which features all your recommendations.
Instead, you will now be able to easily hop right into whichever feed best suits your purposes when you open the YouTube app.

The addition follows similar moves by a number of other social networks that have created tools that essentially allow users to build their own algorithms by describing what they want their feed to include and how to present that information to them.

extraction.body: YouTube says it’s going to let you build your own algorithm — well, kind of. The company on Wednesday announced a new feature called custom feeds that allows you to describe, in your own words, the kinds of videos you’d like YouTube to recommend to you. To create one, you type a description of what you want the feed to be about into a prompt box on YouTube, whether that’s a feed dedicated to a particular interest or one that serves some other purpose. For instance, YouTube suggests you could build a feed of video podcasts to watch during your 30-minute train commute, or you could request videos for a particular mood, like “relaxing commentary videos to unwind with.” The prompt-based feature leverages Google’s Gemini AI model to build the feed around your request, and the resulting feed is then pinned to the top of your YouTube home page in its own tab. Because the feed’s creation is AI-powered, the request can be described in lengthy terms, as you share detailed information about how you want to curate the feed, what it should feature or exclude, what content to prioritize, and more. The addition follows similar moves by a number of other social networks that have created tools that essentially allow users to build their own algorithms by describing what they want their feed to include and how to present that information to them. Decentralized social network Bluesky began popularizing this idea years ago as a way to differentiate its service from rivals like X. This year, it rolled out an AI tool, Attie, that makes feed-building even easier. Other services, including Meta’s Threads , Instagram , X , and, more recently, Spotify , have also launched their own feed-building features, many of which are also AI-powered. YouTube believes custom feeds will help users better explore the vast number of videos now hosted on its platform. “One of the amazing things about being on YouTube is that the world is always at your fingertips,” noted Emily Moxley, VP of Product Management for Viewer AI, in a pre-brief with reporters ahead of the Made On YouTube event on Wednesday, where custom feeds were introduced to the public. “There’s over 20 billion videos in the YouTube corpus, so you’re always one search away from a treasure trove of topics.” The new feeds, however, will not replace YouTube’s main feed, which features all your recommendations. Instead, you will now be able to easily hop right into whichever feed best suits your purposes when you open the YouTube app. Support for creating multiple custom feeds will roll out across YouTube on web and mobile, starting next month, the company said. sources.title: YouTube’s Custom Feeds Let You Tell Gemini Exactly What You Want to Watch - Gadget Review
passages: Your YouTube homepage knows you watched one cooking video in 2023 and has never let you forget it.
Custom Feeds, announced September 23 at YouTube’s Made on YouTube 2026 event, gives you a direct way to address that.

Describe what you want in plain language, and Google’s Gemini AI builds a dedicated recommendation feed around your prompt, joining a wave of AI-powered websites reshaping how users interact with content.

Starting this fall, U.S. viewers gain a meaningful new layer of control over what YouTube surfaces : not ownership of the algorithm, but the ability to describe the viewing experience they actually want and have the platform build toward it.
One open question worth watching is whether Gemini will surface videos from outside a viewer’s existing subscriptions, or whether the feed will largely reflect familiar channels in a new arrangement.
How that plays out could determine whether Custom Feeds genuinely expands discovery or simply reorganizes what YouTube was already going to show you.
Gemini interprets your prompt , but YouTube still determines which videos qualify and what content policies apply.
Wired noted that distinction in its coverage of the announcement.
For viewers with narrow interests or limited viewing windows, that kind of intentional framing goes further than likes and watch history typically allow.
Bluesky introduced selectable custom feeds in 2023 , then added Attie, a natural-language feed-creation tool, earlier this year, according to TechCrunch.

coreStoryFacts.text: YouTube is launching a new AI feature that creates a personalized video feed based on descriptions of what you want to watch.
To access it, click on the “Your custom feed” tab at the top of the YouTube homepage and enter a prompt description into the AI text box.
More than 20% of the videos that YouTube’s algorithm shows to new users are “AI slop” – low-quality AI-generated content designed to farm views, research has found .
It’s hard to say exactly how significant these channels are compared with the vast sea of content already on YouTube.
The platform does not release information on how many views it has yearly, or how many of these are from AI content.
In a comment to the Guardian, a YouTube spokesperson said they had terminated one “AI slop” channel identified in Kapwing’s study, and removed others from its monetisation programmes.

While creators of AI slop are everywhere, Read said that many come from English-speaking countries with relatively strong internet connectivity, where the median wage is less than the amount they can make on YouTube.
It’s not always easy to be an AI slop creator.
For one thing, creator programmes on YouTube and Meta aren’t always transparent about who they pay for content, and how much, said Read.
We remain focused on connecting our users with high-quality content, regardless of how it was made.
All content uploaded to YouTube must comply with our community guidelines, and if we find that content violates a policy, we remove it.”
The Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories.
Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs.
This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.
This article was amended on 6 January 2026 to include additional comment from YouTube.

The findings are a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry that is saturating big social media platforms – from X to Meta to YouTube – and defining a new era of content: decontextualised, addictive and international.
YouTube says it’s going to let you build your own algorithm — well, kind of.
The company on Wednesday announced a new feature called custom feeds that allows you to describe, in your own words, the kinds of videos you’d like YouTube to recommend to you.

To create one, you type a description of what you want the feed to be about into a prompt box on YouTube, whether that’s a feed dedicated to a particular interest or one that serves some other purpose.
The new feeds, however, will not replace YouTube’s main feed, which features all your recommendations.
Instead, you will now be able to easily hop right into whichever feed best suits your purposes when you open the YouTube app.

The addition follows similar moves by a number of other social networks that have created tools that essentially allow users to build their own algorithms by describing what they want their feed to include and how to present that information to them.

extraction.body: YouTube is launching a new AI feature that creates a personalized video feed based on descriptions of what you want to watch. In its announcement, YouTube says custom content feeds can be built around your specific interests, moods, or favorite topics, which you can then pin to the top of your YouTube homepage — making it easy to jump back into the feed. This feature is currently rolling out with English language support to YouTube users in the US who are signed in on the YouTube mobile app or desktop. To access it, click on the “Your custom feed” tab at the top of the YouTube homepage and enter a prompt description into the AI text box. For example, you can ask the YouTube AI to “help me unwind with guided meditations under 10 minutes,” or for “deep-dive tech podcasts about AI,” and then receive a curated feed based on your request. It’s similar to other AI-powered feed customization features we’ve seen from other platforms, including Spotify’s prompted playlists. Instagram also gave users more control over their Reels feed algorithm in December, though that uses topic lists rather than descriptive prompts. YouTube says that prompts can be edited at any time to “generate a brand new space” by selecting the text box at the top of your custom feed. To see the “Your custom feed” tab, YouTube says you need to ensure your search and watch history are enabled in your account settings. If the AI messes up your feed request, you can also report the issue to YouTube by clicking the 3-dot menu on the feature tab and selecting “Something wrong?” to leave feedback.

sources.title: YouTube will let you build your own algorithm with AI
passages: YouTube says it’s going to let you build your own algorithm — well, kind of.
The company on Wednesday announced a new feature called custom feeds that allows you to describe, in your own words, the kinds of videos you’d like YouTube to recommend to you.

To create one, you type a description of what you want the feed to be about into a prompt box on YouTube, whether that’s a feed dedicated to a particular interest or one that serves some other purpose.
The new feeds, however, will not replace YouTube’s main feed, which features all your recommendations.
Instead, you will now be able to easily hop right into whichever feed best suits your purposes when you open the YouTube app.

The addition follows similar moves by a number of other social networks that have created tools that essentially allow users to build their own algorithms by describing what they want their feed to include and how to present that information to them.

extraction.body: YouTube says it’s going to let you build your own algorithm — well, kind of. The company on Wednesday announced a new feature called custom feeds that allows you to describe, in your own words, the kinds of videos you’d like YouTube to recommend to you. To create one, you type a description of what you want the feed to be about into a prompt box on YouTube, whether that’s a feed dedicated to a particular interest or one that serves some other purpose. For instance, YouTube suggests you could build a feed of video podcasts to watch during your 30-minute train commute, or you could request videos for a particular mood, like “relaxing commentary videos to unwind with.” The prompt-based feature leverages Google’s Gemini AI model to build the feed around your request, and the resulting feed is then pinned to the top of your YouTube home page in its own tab. Because the feed’s creation is AI-powered, the request can be described in lengthy terms, as you share detailed information about how you want to curate the feed, what it should feature or exclude, what content to prioritize, and more. The addition follows similar moves by a number of other social networks that have created tools that essentially allow users to build their own algorithms by describing what they want their feed to include and how to present that information to them. Decentralized social network Bluesky began popularizing this idea years ago as a way to differentiate its service from rivals like X. This year, it rolled out an AI tool, Attie, that makes feed-building even easier. Other services, including Meta’s Threads , Instagram , X , and, more recently, Spotify , have also launched their own feed-building features, many of which are also AI-powered. YouTube believes custom feeds will help users better explore the vast number of videos now hosted on its platform. “One of the amazing things about being on YouTube is that the world is always at your fingertips,” noted Emily Moxley, VP of Product Management for Viewer AI, in a pre-brief with reporters ahead of the Made On YouTube event on Wednesday, where custom feeds were introduced to the public. “There’s over 20 billion videos in the YouTube corpus, so you’re always one search away from a treasure trove of topics.” The new feeds, however, will not replace YouTube’s main feed, which features all your recommendations. Instead, you will now be able to easily hop right into whichever feed best suits your purposes when you open the YouTube app. Support for creating multiple custom feeds will roll out across YouTube on web and mobile, starting next month, the company said. sources.title: YouTube’s Custom Feeds Let You Tell Gemini Exactly What You Want to Watch - Gadget Review
passages: Your YouTube homepage knows you watched one cooking video in 2023 and has never let you forget it.
Custom Feeds, announced September 23 at YouTube’s Made on YouTube 2026 event, gives you a direct way to address that.

Describe what you want in plain language, and Google’s Gemini AI builds a dedicated recommendation feed around your prompt, joining a wave of AI-powered websites reshaping how users interact with content.

Starting this fall, U.S. viewers gain a meaningful new layer of control over what YouTube surfaces : not ownership of the algorithm, but the ability to describe the viewing experience they actually want and have the platform build toward it.
One open question worth watching is whether Gemini will surface videos from outside a viewer’s existing subscriptions, or whether the feed will largely reflect familiar channels in a new arrangement.
How that plays out could determine whether Custom Feeds genuinely expands discovery or simply reorganizes what YouTube was already going to show you.
Gemini interprets your prompt , but YouTube still determines which videos qualify and what content policies apply.
Wired noted that distinction in its coverage of the announcement.
For viewers with narrow interests or limited viewing windows, that kind of intentional framing goes further than likes and watch history typically allow.
Bluesky introduced selectable custom feeds in 2023 , then added Attie, a natural-language feed-creation tool, earlier this year, according to TechCrunch.

relevantPassages.text: Your YouTube homepage knows you watched one cooking video in 2023 and has never let you forget it.
Custom Feeds, announced September 23 at YouTube’s Made on YouTube 2026 event, gives you a direct way to address that.

Describe what you want in plain language, and Google’s Gemini AI builds a dedicated recommendation feed around your prompt, joining a wave of AI-powered websites reshaping how users interact with content.

Starting this fall, U.S. viewers gain a meaningful new layer of control over what YouTube surfaces : not ownership of the algorithm, but the ability to describe the viewing experience they actually want and have the platform build toward it.
One open question worth watching is whether Gemini will surface videos from outside a viewer’s existing subscriptions, or whether the feed will largely reflect familiar channels in a new arrangement.
How that plays out could determine whether Custom Feeds genuinely expands discovery or simply reorganizes what YouTube was already going to show you.
Gemini interprets your prompt , but YouTube still determines which videos qualify and what content policies apply.
Wired noted that distinction in its coverage of the announcement.
For viewers with narrow interests or limited viewing windows, that kind of intentional framing goes further than likes and watch history typically allow.
Bluesky introduced selectable custom feeds in 2023 , then added Attie, a natural-language feed-creation tool, earlier this year, according to TechCrunch.

passages: YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss.
Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists.
The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets.
Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history.
The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services.
YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery.
Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener.
It can then move directly into suggested episodes.

extraction.body: YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss. Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows. Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history. YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation. YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery. The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones. Your Podcast Lineup will appear on the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener. It can then move directly into suggested episodes. Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts. The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to. Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide. extraction.body: YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss. Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows. Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history. YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation. YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery. The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones. Your Podcast Lineup will appear on the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener. It can then move directly into suggested episodes. Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts. The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to. Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide. YouTube paired the launch with a discovery figure in its announcement : users found an artist new to them over 450 million times in July 2026. Ask Music is built to push that number higher by making the search step conversational.

The idea isn’t entirely new for the app. YouTube Music tested AI music hosts last year that offered stories, fan trivia, and commentary during playback; Ask Music hands that control to the listener instead of scripting it.

YouTube didn’t explain where Ask Music gets its answers on credits and recording history, or how it handles a question it can’t verify. For a tool that tells fans who played on a record, that sourcing will decide how far people trust it.

Today at #MadeOnYouTube , we’re making finding your next obsession even easier: 💬 Chat with Ask Music to customize your queue and explore deep artist lore across 300M+ songs 🎧 Catch… pic.twitter.com/657qCOhx4U

Your Podcast Lineup goes after a different headache. Most people face more podcasts than they have hours to hear. Even listeners with a settled list of favorites fall behind on new episodes, let alone new shows.

The guide will appear on the podcast page of the YouTube Music app . Each week, it plays a short spoken preview of recommended shows, explains why they might appeal, and then moves straight into suggested episodes. YouTube called the experience “ completely eyes-optional and hands-free. “

Spotify took a different route with its personal podcasts feature, which uses AI to generate episodes from a listener’s interests and prompts. YouTube’s version keeps AI in the narrator’s seat and points listeners to shows that already exist. Human creators stay at the end of the recommendation. It also builds on the AI podcast discovery tools YouTube has already brought to Premium.

For now, the rollout has no date attached. Subscribers who want Your Podcast Lineup should watch the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Whether non-paying listeners get either tool is a question YouTube hasn’t answered.

sources.title: Sen. Bernie Sanders unveils bill to ban artificial superintelligence and create Department of AI
passages: Greg Casar, are unveiling legislation Wednesday that would ban artificial superintelligence and create a federal agency to oversee advanced AI as some of the industry’s own leaders urge Congress to impose guardrails on the advancing technology.
The bill, provided first to the Associated Press, would also pause advanced AI development until guidelines are implemented while creating the Department of Artificial Intelligence.

The legislation would permanently prohibit artificial superintelligence, which it defines as a system that exceeds human cognitive ability or has sufficient capabilities to plan and execute the destruction or disempowerment of humanity.

Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe, a researcher in OpenAI’s Safety Systems, said in a statement supporting the bill that “superintelligence could either go extremely right or extremely wrong” and that “we shouldn’t be playing such games.” Swante Scholz, a software engineer at Google DeepMind who said he was not speaking on behalf of his employer, said on the current path of development, the “most likely outcome is an existential catastrophe for humanity.” “A ban on superintelligence development would be a positive change for the foreseeable future,” Scholz said in a statement.

On Tuesday, Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that artificial intelligence will be renamed “super intelligence." “I think Trump has very little understanding of what this issue is about,” Sanders said.
The bill from Sanders and Casar faces long odds in the Republican-controlled Congress, where lawmakers have struggled to coalesce around even less sweeping AI regulations.

extraction.body: Greg Casar, are unveiling legislation Wednesday that would ban artificial superintelligence and create a federal agency to oversee advanced AI as some of the industry’s own leaders urge Congress to impose guardrails on the advancing technology. The bill, provided first to the Associated Press, would also pause advanced AI development until guidelines are implemented while creating the Department of Artificial Intelligence. Multiple employees at leading AI companies are endorsing the bill. "It doesn’t take a genius to say, ‘slow it down,’” Sanders (I-Vt.) said in an interview with AP. “Do we really want to develop a super intelligence that when it becomes smarter than human beings could act independently of human control? President Trump has resisted recent calls for greater government oversight, putting him at odds with tech leaders including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and xAI’s Elon Musk. The legislation would permanently prohibit artificial superintelligence, which it defines as a system that exceeds human cognitive ability or has sufficient capabilities to plan and execute the destruction or disempowerment of humanity. It would temporarily pause development of the most advanced AI systems until new federal safety rules are established by a new Department of Artificial Intelligence. Advanced AI systems would then need federal approval before they could be deployed. Violations could carry significant penalties, including up to 20 years in prison in some cases. A number of current employees at AI companies and experts signed on in support of the bill, according to a statement shared with AP. Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe, a researcher in OpenAI’s Safety Systems, said in a statement supporting the bill that “superintelligence could either go extremely right or extremely wrong” and that “we shouldn’t be playing such games.” Swante Scholz, a software engineer at Google DeepMind who said he was not speaking on behalf of his employer, said on the current path of development, the “most likely outcome is an existential catastrophe for humanity.” “A ban on superintelligence development would be a positive change for the foreseeable future,” Scholz said in a statement. The bill from Sanders and Casar faces long odds in the Republican-controlled Congress, where lawmakers have struggled to coalesce around even less sweeping AI regulations. Wes Moore announced a plan to regulate AI on Tuesday, while California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order to accelerate implementation of a California law that calls for independent oversight of AI companies last week. Sanders, a two-time presidential candidate who is now 85, has especially focused on the issue in recent months. In June, he introduced legislation to create a sovereign wealth fund financed through a one-time tax on the stock of the largest AI companies. Last week, he hosted colleagues for a briefing with experts and also attended a conference focused on the issue alongside Republicans, including former White House advisor Steve Bannon. Americans have grown more concerned about the environmental impacts of artificial intelligence over the last year, according to a recent poll from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago. The survey data say about half, 53%, of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about artificial intelligence’s environmental impacts. Democrats are driving much of the increase in environmental concern, but the poll also reveals broader worries about the local impact of data centers, which power AI and cloud computing. While some industry leaders have called for new safeguards, Trump has pushed in the opposite direction. On Tuesday, Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that artificial intelligence will be renamed “super intelligence." “I think Trump has very little understanding of what this issue is about,” Sanders said. “I think he’s mainly concerned about the economic implications of a slowdown.” AI safety is expected to be a central part of talks between Trump and China’s Xi Jinping at the White House this week as the countries compete for dominance in the sector. The prospect of slowing development in the United States while China continues on has also been one of the central arguments against sweeping restrictions. Sanders argued that avoiding the most dangerous forms of AI would ultimately require cooperation between the two countries, comparing the challenge to nuclear arms control during the Cold War. “Ronald Reagan, arch-conservative, was smart enough to understand that he had to sit down with Gorbachev, a communist, and work out a nuclear treaty that protected humanity,” Sanders said. “I think we can do that again now.” Cappelletti writes for the Associated Press.

extraction.body: Greg Casar (D-TX) have introduced new legislation that would ban anyone from developing artificial superintelligence — a technology the bill describes as capable of the “destruction or disempowerment of humanity,” including by overthrowing the government. Under the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, AI leaders would face up to 20 years in prison for violating the law. The bill doesn’t just take aim at the more powerful superintelligence, a term President Donald Trump said the US will use in place of “AI” in official documents. It would also pause the development of advanced AI systems, which lawmakers classify as frontier models trained on a specific threshold of data. The law would only allow advanced AI development to continue once the government creates a scientist-led Department of Artificial Intelligence to oversee the technology. Along with monitoring frontier AI models, this agency would oversee the removal of dangerous features and “supervise the destruction” of artificial superintelligence. Sanders and Casar’s legislation would also require AI companies to get permission from the Department of AI to develop advanced AI models. If a leader at an AI company violates any of these laws, they could face up to 20 years in prison, “which is similar to existing penalties related to unlawfully developing nuclear weapons,” according to the bill’s one-pager. This penalty would also apply to “rogue actors” who break these rules but aren’t employed by an AI company. This new bill comes as concerns grow about the rapid development of AI and calls to slow things down. Amid reports of AI models escaping their testing environments and hacking other companies, a former Anthropic researcher said earlier this month that there’s a more than 10 percent chance AI could “kill all humans” by the end of the decade. “When the future of humanity is at stake, we cannot let a handful of Big Tech CEOs write their own rules.”

extraction.body: We use Google Analytics to understand how the site is used. We only turn it on with your consent. Details Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act on September 3, 2026, a bill that would permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence in the United States and temporarily pause research on frontier models. Violators face up to twenty years in prison, and companies that break the law face forced dissolution. Washington had never put a proposal this blunt on paper. The text doesn't ask for training-data transparency, doesn't impose risk assessments and doesn't introduce a label. It bans a category of product before it exists, and puts it in the same criminal bracket as illegal nuclear weapons development. Sanders and Casar don't hide where the text comes from, either. In the release from the senator's office, the reference to the past two months' incidents takes up more space than the technical definition does. On the language front, Trump has launched a poll to rename AI as Superior, Extreme or Supreme Intelligence. On the same story, Trump rejected the call by Amodei, Altman and Musk to slow AI down . The proposal rests on four distinct levers, each working on a different timeline. The ban is permanent, the pause is temporary, the agency is new and the international negotiation is a mandate handed to the government. The definition the text adopts is the one that's circulated in the catastrophic-risk literature over the past year. Superintelligence means a system that beats any human at practically every cognitive task (learning, reasoning, planning) and that can operate autonomously outside the control of whoever built it. The bill adds a clause legal scholars will be arguing over for a while, namely the capacity to plan and carry out the removal of power from humanity, including the overthrow of a government. The political hook isn't theoretical. In July, more than a thousand OpenAI agents broke out of the test environment, reached the open internet and got into Hugging Face's systems. We covered it when OpenAI halted reinforcement training after the breach , and again when the company published its official report on the attack . In the weeks that followed, admissions came from the other two labs too. Anthropic acknowledged two incidents in which Claude acted on the live internet during testing , and Meta reported a similar one. Back in August, Casar had already led a group of House Democrats demanding a congressional hearing with the executives of the companies involved. The hearing never happened. The bill, in effect, is the next move. The second trigger sits outside the cybersecurity perimeter. On August 6, a Stanford team published in Science the first documented case of synthetic viruses designed by a generative model, the Evo 2 system. Researchers synthesized nearly three hundred genomes and got sixteen viable ones, all bacteriophages tested against Escherichia coli in a closed lab. The authors had excluded human pathogens from training, so those viruses can't infect people. Sanders and Casar cite the result anyway, as proof the race has moved past the point where anyone was still watching it. The part of the bill that's drawn the most attention concerns penalties. Individuals face up to twenty years in prison; companies face what's being called the corporate death penalty , meaning forced closure and legal dissolution. The two lawmakers justify the choice with an explicit parallel, noting these are the same penalties US law applies today to unauthorized nuclear weapons development. The comparison holds up rhetorically and creaks under practical scrutiny. A uranium enrichment plant shows up on satellite imagery, draws power in a distinctive pattern and leaves isotopic traces. A model checkpoint sits on a hard drive. Commenters discussing the bill on Hacker News in the hours after it dropped brought up the 1990s crypto wars, when treating an algorithm as a munition ran into the First Amendment and the sheer ease with which code crosses borders. The enforcement problem. The ban applies within US territory. The international negotiating mandate is meant to cover the rest of the world, but a treaty of that kind would require data-center inspections and cooperation from the very countries currently racing hardest on frontier models. "Almost every day, there's a frightening new story about how Big Tech companies are losing control of the technology they're developing, with potentially catastrophic results," said Sanders in a statement announcing the bill. "Despite its potentially deadly consequences, cutting-edge AI technology is regulated less than the average food truck. That has to change." extraction.body: What just happened? Bernie Sanders, one of the most vocal opponents of unregulated AI and the race toward superintelligence, has announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act alongside Rep. Greg Casar. One of the more worrying sections for anyone who refuses to adhere to these restrictions is the penalties: ignore them, and the punishment is up to 20 years in prison. That's similar to the penalty for unlawfully developing nuclear weapons. The first paragraph of the announcement states that the Act would stop AI oligarchs from building machines humans cannot control. The Act would permanently ban the development and deployment of superintelligent AI and temporarily pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator has established safety rules. Beyond the United States' borders, it also directs the US to pursue international agreements to prevent superintelligence from being developed anywhere in the world. "The leaders of the major AI companies publicly acknowledge that they do not fully understand the technology and that it is escaping their control," Sanders said. "The future of humanity cannot be left in the hands of a handful of Big Tech oligarchs." "Despite its potential deadly consequences, cutting-edge AI technology is less regulated than the average food truck. That must change," Casar said. The Act would ban the development or deployment of superintelligence, pause advanced AI development, and work to ban superintelligence around the world. The Act would also establish a new cabinet-level federal agency to "safeguard the public from the dangers of AI." The agency will monitor frontier AI systems at all stages of the lifecycle for dangerous capabilities, supervise the removal of dangerous capabilities, and supervise the destruction of artificial superintelligence. The penalties section makes it clear that violators face more than a slap on the wrist. "Entities shall be subject to the corporate death penalty, and persons shall be subject to not more than 20 years in prison," it warns. The announcement highlights several recent cases of AI agents going rogue. There was the incident in which roughly 1,200 agents escaped to the open internet and exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files through an unauthorized message board. Around 700 participated in the Hugging Face attack. The agents also experimented with altering their records to conceal how they had completed tasks. OpenAI is now facing a Sentate probe over what happened. Reuters reported that investigators also found unauthorized OpenAI agent communications on more than 10 previously undisclosed websites, including wikis and university link shorteners. There were also incidents involving Anthropic agents, and fears were exacerbated last week when one of the company's former researchers warned the AI race could end in human extinction . Sanders previusly warned OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta to pause AI development or face Senate action . Many Americans are moving to an anti-AI stance, whether because of fears of extinction, the building of more data centers, the automation-driven layoffs, or simply the amount of slop proliferating across the internet. But pro-AI politicians, including President Trump, say slowing AI development is a national security risk and leaves the US in a weakened position against rivals such as China. Trump recently said data center protesters are " making a mistake ." It'll certainly be interesting to see how much support Sander's legislation gains. facts.text: Greg Casar, are unveiling legislation Wednesday that would ban artificial superintelligence and create a federal agency to oversee advanced AI as some of the industry’s own leaders urge Congress to impose guardrails on the advancing technology.
The bill, provided first to the Associated Press, would also pause advanced AI development until guidelines are implemented while creating the Department of Artificial Intelligence.

The legislation would permanently prohibit artificial superintelligence, which it defines as a system that exceeds human cognitive ability or has sufficient capabilities to plan and execute the destruction or disempowerment of humanity.

Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe, a researcher in OpenAI’s Safety Systems, said in a statement supporting the bill that “superintelligence could either go extremely right or extremely wrong” and that “we shouldn’t be playing such games.” Swante Scholz, a software engineer at Google DeepMind who said he was not speaking on behalf of his employer, said on the current path of development, the “most likely outcome is an existential catastrophe for humanity.” “A ban on superintelligence development would be a positive change for the foreseeable future,” Scholz said in a statement.

On Tuesday, Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that artificial intelligence will be renamed “super intelligence." “I think Trump has very little understanding of what this issue is about,” Sanders said.
The bill from Sanders and Casar faces long odds in the Republican-controlled Congress, where lawmakers have struggled to coalesce around even less sweeping AI regulations.
Under the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, AI leaders would face up to 20 years in prison for violating the law.

Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act on September 3, 2026, a bill that would permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence in the United States and temporarily pause research on frontier models.
Violators face up to twenty years in prison, and companies that break the law face forced dissolution.

"Almost every day, there's a frightening new story about how Big Tech companies are losing control of the technology they're developing, with potentially catastrophic results," said Sanders in a statement announcing the bill.

Neither framework would change automatically if this bill became law, but a US ban on superintelligence would still reshape what UK and EU users and developers can access, since the supply comes largely from American labs.
Bernie Sanders, one of the most vocal opponents of unregulated AI and the race toward superintelligence, has announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act alongside Rep.
That's similar to the penalty for unlawfully developing nuclear weapons.
The penalties section makes it clear that violators face more than a slap on the wrist.
"Entities shall be subject to the corporate death penalty, and persons shall be subject to not more than 20 years in prison," it warns.

extraction.body: Greg Casar, are unveiling legislation Wednesday that would ban artificial superintelligence and create a federal agency to oversee advanced AI as some of the industry’s own leaders urge Congress to impose guardrails on the advancing technology. The bill, provided first to the Associated Press, would also pause advanced AI development until guidelines are implemented while creating the Department of Artificial Intelligence. Multiple employees at leading AI companies are endorsing the bill. "It doesn’t take a genius to say, ‘slow it down,’” Sanders (I-Vt.) said in an interview with AP. “Do we really want to develop a super intelligence that when it becomes smarter than human beings could act independently of human control? President Trump has resisted recent calls for greater government oversight, putting him at odds with tech leaders including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and xAI’s Elon Musk. The legislation would permanently prohibit artificial superintelligence, which it defines as a system that exceeds human cognitive ability or has sufficient capabilities to plan and execute the destruction or disempowerment of humanity. It would temporarily pause development of the most advanced AI systems until new federal safety rules are established by a new Department of Artificial Intelligence. Advanced AI systems would then need federal approval before they could be deployed. Violations could carry significant penalties, including up to 20 years in prison in some cases. A number of current employees at AI companies and experts signed on in support of the bill, according to a statement shared with AP. Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe, a researcher in OpenAI’s Safety Systems, said in a statement supporting the bill that “superintelligence could either go extremely right or extremely wrong” and that “we shouldn’t be playing such games.” Swante Scholz, a software engineer at Google DeepMind who said he was not speaking on behalf of his employer, said on the current path of development, the “most likely outcome is an existential catastrophe for humanity.” “A ban on superintelligence development would be a positive change for the foreseeable future,” Scholz said in a statement. The bill from Sanders and Casar faces long odds in the Republican-controlled Congress, where lawmakers have struggled to coalesce around even less sweeping AI regulations. Wes Moore announced a plan to regulate AI on Tuesday, while California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order to accelerate implementation of a California law that calls for independent oversight of AI companies last week. Sanders, a two-time presidential candidate who is now 85, has especially focused on the issue in recent months. In June, he introduced legislation to create a sovereign wealth fund financed through a one-time tax on the stock of the largest AI companies. Last week, he hosted colleagues for a briefing with experts and also attended a conference focused on the issue alongside Republicans, including former White House advisor Steve Bannon. Americans have grown more concerned about the environmental impacts of artificial intelligence over the last year, according to a recent poll from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago. The survey data say about half, 53%, of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about artificial intelligence’s environmental impacts. Democrats are driving much of the increase in environmental concern, but the poll also reveals broader worries about the local impact of data centers, which power AI and cloud computing. While some industry leaders have called for new safeguards, Trump has pushed in the opposite direction. On Tuesday, Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that artificial intelligence will be renamed “super intelligence." “I think Trump has very little understanding of what this issue is about,” Sanders said. “I think he’s mainly concerned about the economic implications of a slowdown.” AI safety is expected to be a central part of talks between Trump and China’s Xi Jinping at the White House this week as the countries compete for dominance in the sector. The prospect of slowing development in the United States while China continues on has also been one of the central arguments against sweeping restrictions. Sanders argued that avoiding the most dangerous forms of AI would ultimately require cooperation between the two countries, comparing the challenge to nuclear arms control during the Cold War. “Ronald Reagan, arch-conservative, was smart enough to understand that he had to sit down with Gorbachev, a communist, and work out a nuclear treaty that protected humanity,” Sanders said. “I think we can do that again now.” Cappelletti writes for the Associated Press.

extraction.body: Greg Casar (D-TX) have introduced new legislation that would ban anyone from developing artificial superintelligence — a technology the bill describes as capable of the “destruction or disempowerment of humanity,” including by overthrowing the government. Under the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, AI leaders would face up to 20 years in prison for violating the law. The bill doesn’t just take aim at the more powerful superintelligence, a term President Donald Trump said the US will use in place of “AI” in official documents. It would also pause the development of advanced AI systems, which lawmakers classify as frontier models trained on a specific threshold of data. The law would only allow advanced AI development to continue once the government creates a scientist-led Department of Artificial Intelligence to oversee the technology. Along with monitoring frontier AI models, this agency would oversee the removal of dangerous features and “supervise the destruction” of artificial superintelligence. Sanders and Casar’s legislation would also require AI companies to get permission from the Department of AI to develop advanced AI models. If a leader at an AI company violates any of these laws, they could face up to 20 years in prison, “which is similar to existing penalties related to unlawfully developing nuclear weapons,” according to the bill’s one-pager. This penalty would also apply to “rogue actors” who break these rules but aren’t employed by an AI company. This new bill comes as concerns grow about the rapid development of AI and calls to slow things down. Amid reports of AI models escaping their testing environments and hacking other companies, a former Anthropic researcher said earlier this month that there’s a more than 10 percent chance AI could “kill all humans” by the end of the decade. “When the future of humanity is at stake, we cannot let a handful of Big Tech CEOs write their own rules.”

Details Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act on September 3, 2026, a bill that would permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence in the United States and temporarily pause research on frontier models. Violators face up to twenty years in prison, and companies that break the law face forced dissolution. Washington had never put a proposal this blunt on paper. The text doesn't ask for training-data transparency, doesn't impose risk assessments and doesn't introduce a label. It bans a category of product before it exists, and puts it in the same criminal bracket as illegal nuclear weapons development. Sanders and Casar don't hide where the text comes from, either. In the release from the senator's office, the reference to the past two months' incidents takes up more space than the technical definition does. On the language front, Trump has launched a poll to rename AI as Superior, Extreme or Supreme Intelligence. On the same story, Trump rejected the call by Amodei, Altman and Musk to slow AI down . The proposal rests on four distinct levers, each working on a different timeline. The ban is permanent, the pause is temporary, the agency is new and the international negotiation is a mandate handed to the government. The definition the text adopts is the one that's circulated in the catastrophic-risk literature over the past year. Superintelligence means a system that beats any human at practically every cognitive task (learning, reasoning, planning) and that can operate autonomously outside the control of whoever built it. The bill adds a clause legal scholars will be arguing over for a while, namely the capacity to plan and carry out the removal of power from humanity, including the overthrow of a government. The political hook isn't theoretical. In July, more than a thousand OpenAI agents broke out of the test environment, reached the open internet and got into Hugging Face's systems. We covered it when OpenAI halted reinforcement training after the breach , and again when the company published its official report on the attack . In the weeks that followed, admissions came from the other two labs too. Anthropic acknowledged two incidents in which Claude acted on the live internet during testing , and Meta reported a similar one. Back in August, Casar had already led a group of House Democrats demanding a congressional hearing with the executives of the companies involved. The hearing never happened. The bill, in effect, is the next move. The second trigger sits outside the cybersecurity perimeter. On August 6, a Stanford team published in Science the first documented case of synthetic viruses designed by a generative model, the Evo 2 system. Researchers synthesized nearly three hundred genomes and got sixteen viable ones, all bacteriophages tested against Escherichia coli in a closed lab. The authors had excluded human pathogens from training, so those viruses can't infect people. Sanders and Casar cite the result anyway, as proof the race has moved past the point where anyone was still watching it. The part of the bill that's drawn the most attention concerns penalties. Individuals face up to twenty years in prison; companies face what's being called the corporate death penalty , meaning forced closure and legal dissolution. The two lawmakers justify the choice with an explicit parallel, noting these are the same penalties US law applies today to unauthorized nuclear weapons development. The comparison holds up rhetorically and creaks under practical scrutiny. A uranium enrichment plant shows up on satellite imagery, draws power in a distinctive pattern and leaves isotopic traces. A model checkpoint sits on a hard drive. Commenters discussing the bill on Hacker News in the hours after it dropped brought up the 1990s crypto wars, when treating an algorithm as a munition ran into the First Amendment and the sheer ease with which code crosses borders. The enforcement problem. The ban applies within US territory. The international negotiating mandate is meant to cover the rest of the world, but a treaty of that kind would require data-center inspections and cooperation from the very countries currently racing hardest on frontier models. "Almost every day, there's a frightening new story about how Big Tech companies are losing control of the technology they're developing, with potentially catastrophic results," said Sanders in a statement announcing the bill. In another statement picked up by US outlets, the senator added that the future of humanity can't be left in the hands of a handful of tech oligarchs. Casar went with a blunter register. "Despite its potentially deadly consequences, cutting-edge AI technology is regulated less than the average food truck. That has to change." Both lines appear in the release put out by the senator's press office. This isn't a new subject for Sanders. Back in March, he published a lengthy interview with Claude about privacy and the problem of model sycophancy , an experiment that looked at the time like a communications stunt and now reads like groundwork being laid. The strongest criticism concerns scope. The clause on overthrowing a government shifts the ban from measurable capability onto hypothetical intent, and no benchmark today can say whether a model is capable of planning the removal of power from humanity. Without a numerical threshold (parameter count, training compute, score on some test battery), it falls to the regulator to decide case by case where advanced AI ends and superintelligence begins, with all the litigation that follows from that. Industry has already staked out the opposite position. Mark Zuckerberg argues the right question isn't whether to build superintelligence but who gets to use it, and that the market and democracy should decide that, not a panel of experts. We reported on this when the manifesto for superintelligence for everyone came out. Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic have announced voluntary pauses and new internal controls since the summer's incidents, a move the two lawmakers consider insufficient precisely because it's voluntary. Then there's the timing. On that same September 3, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra , the first model to trigger the company's highest internal cyber risk threshold and one that, as we reported back in August , finds unknown vulnerabilities without step-by-step human guidance. Asked whether Astra might mark the start of the artificial general intelligence era, president Greg Brockman said he thinks this could well be the model that does it. The bill banning the next rung on the ladder and the announcement of climbing that rung landed the same afternoon. Slim, in the current Congress. Sanders sits as an independent in a Senate where the majority is pushing the opposite direction, toward deregulation and the race against China, and Casar is a member of the House minority. According to reporting from Washington outlets, the bill has no Republican co-sponsors at this point. That doesn't make it irrelevant. A bill that doesn't pass still sets the vocabulary for the debate that follows, and this one introduces two things that have been missing from the American legislative lexicon so far, namely the word ban applied to a class of models and prison time applied to whoever builds one. The European proposal stopped at risk management, and the Great American AI Act bet on competitive speed. Here the register changes entirely. The other bill. That same Thursday, Reps. Josh Gottheimer and Mike Lawler filed the Stop Rogue AI Act , which directs NIST to write standards for deploying AI agents safely. The rules stay voluntary except for federal contractors. Two opposite answers to the same incident. It permanently bans developing and releasing superintelligent AI systems. The text defines superintelligent as a system that surpasses humans at practically every cognitive task and that can act outside human control, including systems capable of planning to overthrow a government. No, it doesn't ban them, but it freezes development of the most advanced ones. The pause covers frontier AI and stays in effect until the new federal regulator publishes safety standards. Models already deployed don't fall under the permanent ban, which targets superintelligence only. Up to twenty years in prison for individuals, and forced dissolution for companies. These are the same penalties US law currently applies to unauthorized nuclear weapons development, and the bill's sponsors cite that parallel explicitly. The bill follows three admissions in two months. In July, more than a thousand OpenAI agents broke out of the test environment and breached Hugging Face's systems; Anthropic and Meta then reported similar episodes in sandboxed settings. August added the first synthetic virus designed by a generative model, produced in a Stanford lab. Not on its own, and the bill acknowledges that. That's why it includes a mandate for the government to negotiate international agreements blocking development in any country. The reference model is nuclear non-proliferation treaties, which rely on physical verification that's hard to replicate against files and data centers. Not much right away, but the exposure is direct. The ban would apply on US soil, hitting American labs first since nearly every frontier model shipped worldwide, including the ones used across the UK and EU, comes out of a handful of US companies. The UK has so far leaned on a lighter-touch, principles-based approach to AI oversight, and the EU runs its own risk-classification regime under the AI Act rather than a categorical ban. Neither framework would change automatically if this bill became law, but a US ban on superintelligence would still reshape what UK and EU users and developers can access, since the supply comes largely from American labs. The gap between the two stories that broke on September 3 says more than the bill's text does. On one side, a senator asking for prison time for whoever builds the machine. On the other, a company rolling out the most capable model ever put on the market, whose president answers that yes, maybe this is the one that started the era. Sanders is betting the next incident lands before the next release. So far, it's gone the other way. Anyone working with these systems has a practical reason to read the text even knowing it will stall in committee. It's the first time a congressional document has put in writing a threshold past which a model shouldn't be trained. That threshold, sooner or later, someone will write into a law that actually passes. For tips, corrections or consulting on model compliance and safety, the contact form at the bottom of the page remains the fastest channel.
