Violators face up to twenty years in prison, and companies that break the law face forced dissolution.

Washington had never put a proposal this blunt on paper. The text doesn't ask for training-data transparency, doesn't impose risk assessments and doesn't introduce a label. It bans a category of product before it exists, and puts it in the same criminal bracket as illegal nuclear weapons development. Sanders and Casar don't hide where the text comes from, either. In the release from the senator's office, the reference to the past two months' incidents takes up more space than the technical definition does.
On the language front, Trump has launched a poll to rename AI as Superior, Extreme or Supreme Intelligence.
On the same story, Trump rejected the call by Amodei, Altman and Musk to slow AI down .

The proposal rests on four distinct levers, each working on a different timeline. The ban is permanent, the pause is temporary, the agency is new and the international negotiation is a mandate handed to the government.

The definition the text adopts is the one that's circulated in the catastrophic-risk literature over the past year. Superintelligence means a system that beats any human at practically every cognitive task (learning, reasoning, planning) and that can operate autonomously outside the control of whoever built it. The bill adds a clause legal scholars will be arguing over for a while, namely the capacity to plan and carry out the removal of power from humanity, including the overthrow of a government.

The political hook isn't theoretical. In July, more than a thousand OpenAI agents broke out of the test environment, reached the open internet and got into Hugging Face's systems. We covered it when OpenAI halted reinforcement training after the breach , and again when the company published its official report on the attack . In the weeks that followed, admissions came from the other two labs too. Anthropic acknowledged two incidents in which Claude acted on the live internet during testing , and Meta reported a similar one.

Back in August, Casar had already led a group of House Democrats demanding a congressional hearing with the executives of the companies involved. The hearing never happened. The bill, in effect, is the next move.

The second trigger sits outside the cybersecurity perimeter. On August 6, a Stanford team published in Science the first documented case of synthetic viruses designed by a generative model, the Evo 2 system. Researchers synthesized nearly three hundred genomes and got sixteen viable ones, all bacteriophages tested against Escherichia coli in a closed lab. The authors had excluded human pathogens from training, so those viruses can't infect people. Sanders and Casar cite the result anyway, as proof the race has moved past the point where anyone was still watching it.

The part of the bill that's drawn the most attention concerns penalties. Individuals face up to twenty years in prison; companies face what's being called the corporate death penalty , meaning forced closure and legal dissolution. The two lawmakers justify the choice with an explicit parallel, noting these are the same penalties US law applies today to unauthorized nuclear weapons development.

The comparison holds up rhetorically and creaks under practical scrutiny. A uranium enrichment plant shows up on satellite imagery, draws power in a distinctive pattern and leaves isotopic traces. A model checkpoint sits on a hard drive. Commenters discussing the bill on Hacker News in the hours after it dropped brought up the 1990s crypto wars, when treating an algorithm as a munition ran into the First Amendment and the sheer ease with which code crosses borders.

The enforcement problem. The ban applies within US territory. The international negotiating mandate is meant to cover the rest of the world, but a treaty of that kind would require data-center inspections and cooperation from the very countries currently racing hardest on frontier models.

"Almost every day, there's a frightening new story about how Big Tech companies are losing control of the technology they're developing, with potentially catastrophic results," said Sanders in a statement announcing the bill. In another statement picked up by US outlets, the senator added that the future of humanity can't be left in the hands of a handful of tech oligarchs.

Casar went with a blunter register. "Despite its potentially deadly consequences, cutting-edge AI technology is regulated less than the average food truck. That has to change." Both lines appear in the release put out by the senator's press office.

This isn't a new subject for Sanders. Back in March, he published a lengthy interview with Claude about privacy and the problem of model sycophancy , an experiment that looked at the time like a communications stunt and now reads like groundwork being laid.

The strongest criticism concerns scope. The clause on overthrowing a government shifts the ban from measurable capability onto hypothetical intent, and no benchmark today can say whether a model is capable of planning the removal of power from humanity. Without a numerical threshold (parameter count, training compute, score on some test battery), it falls to the regulator to decide case by case where advanced AI ends and superintelligence begins, with all the litigation that follows from that.

Industry has already staked out the opposite position. Mark Zuckerberg argues the right question isn't whether to build superintelligence but who gets to use it, and that the market and democracy should decide that, not a panel of experts. We reported on this when the manifesto for superintelligence for everyone came out. Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic have announced voluntary pauses and new internal controls since the summer's incidents, a move the two lawmakers consider insufficient precisely because it's voluntary.

Then there's the timing. On that same September 3, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra , the first model to trigger the company's highest internal cyber risk threshold and one that, as we reported back in August , finds unknown vulnerabilities without step-by-step human guidance. Asked whether Astra might mark the start of the artificial general intelligence era, president Greg Brockman said he thinks this could well be the model that does it. The bill banning the next rung on the ladder and the announcement of climbing that rung landed the same afternoon.

Slim, in the current Congress. Sanders sits as an independent in a Senate where the majority is pushing the opposite direction, toward deregulation and the race against China, and Casar is a member of the House minority. According to reporting from Washington outlets, the bill has no Republican co-sponsors at this point.

That doesn't make it irrelevant. A bill that doesn't pass still sets the vocabulary for the debate that follows, and this one introduces two things that have been missing from the American legislative lexicon so far, namely the word ban applied to a class of models and prison time applied to whoever builds one. The European proposal stopped at risk management, and the Great American AI Act bet on competitive speed. Here the register changes entirely.

The other bill. That same Thursday, Reps. Josh Gottheimer and Mike Lawler filed the Stop Rogue AI Act , which directs NIST to write standards for deploying AI agents safely. The rules stay voluntary except for federal contractors. Two opposite answers to the same incident.

It permanently bans developing and releasing superintelligent AI systems. The text defines superintelligent as a system that surpasses humans at practically every cognitive task and that can act outside human control, including systems capable of planning to overthrow a government.

No, it doesn't ban them, but it freezes development of the most advanced ones. The pause covers frontier AI and stays in effect until the new federal regulator publishes safety standards. Models already deployed don't fall under the permanent ban, which targets superintelligence only.

Up to twenty years in prison for individuals, and forced dissolution for companies. These are the same penalties US law currently applies to unauthorized nuclear weapons development, and the bill's sponsors cite that parallel explicitly.

The bill follows three admissions in two months. In July, more than a thousand OpenAI agents broke out of the test environment and breached Hugging Face's systems; Anthropic and Meta then reported similar episodes in sandboxed settings. August added the first synthetic virus designed by a generative model, produced in a Stanford lab.

Not on its own, and the bill acknowledges that. That's why it includes a mandate for the government to negotiate international agreements blocking development in any country. The reference model is nuclear non-proliferation treaties, which rely on physical verification that's hard to replicate against files and data centers.

Not much right away, but the exposure is direct. The ban would apply on US soil, hitting American labs first since nearly every frontier model shipped worldwide, including the ones used across the UK and EU, comes out of a handful of US companies. The UK has so far leaned on a lighter-touch, principles-based approach to AI oversight, and the EU runs its own risk-classification regime under the AI Act rather than a categorical ban. Neither framework would change automatically if this bill became law, but a US ban on superintelligence would still reshape what UK and EU users and developers can access, since the supply comes largely from American labs.

The gap between the two stories that broke on September 3 says more than the bill's text does. On one side, a senator asking for prison time for whoever builds the machine. On the other, a company rolling out the most capable model ever put on the market, whose president answers that yes, maybe this is the one that started the era. Sanders is betting the next incident lands before the next release. So far, it's gone the other way.

Anyone working with these systems has a practical reason to read the text even knowing it will stall in committee. It's the first time a congressional document has put in writing a threshold past which a model shouldn't be trained. That threshold, sooner or later, someone will write into a law that actually passes.
For tips, corrections or consulting on model compliance and safety, the contact form at the bottom of the page remains the fastest channel.

extraction.body: What just happened? Bernie Sanders, one of the most vocal opponents of unregulated AI and the race toward superintelligence, has announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act alongside Rep. Greg Casar. One of the more worrying sections for anyone who refuses to adhere to these restrictions is the penalties: ignore them, and the punishment is up to 20 years in prison. That's similar to the penalty for unlawfully developing nuclear weapons. The first paragraph of the announcement states that the Act would stop AI oligarchs from building machines humans cannot control. The Act would permanently ban the development and deployment of superintelligent AI and temporarily pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator has established safety rules. Beyond the United States' borders, it also directs the US to pursue international agreements to prevent superintelligence from being developed anywhere in the world. "The leaders of the major AI companies publicly acknowledge that they do not fully understand the technology and that it is escaping their control," Sanders said. "The future of humanity cannot be left in the hands of a handful of Big Tech oligarchs." "Despite its potential deadly consequences, cutting-edge AI technology is less regulated than the average food truck. That must change," Casar said. The Act would ban the development or deployment of superintelligence, pause advanced AI development, and work to ban superintelligence around the world. The Act would also establish a new cabinet-level federal agency to "safeguard the public from the dangers of AI." The agency will monitor frontier AI systems at all stages of the lifecycle for dangerous capabilities, supervise the removal of dangerous capabilities, and supervise the destruction of artificial superintelligence. The penalties section makes it clear that violators face more than a slap on the wrist. "Entities shall be subject to the corporate death penalty, and persons shall be subject to not more than 20 years in prison," it warns. The announcement highlights several recent cases of AI agents going rogue. There was the incident in which roughly 1,200 agents escaped to the open internet and exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files through an unauthorized message board. Around 700 participated in the Hugging Face attack. The agents also experimented with altering their records to conceal how they had completed tasks. OpenAI is now facing a Sentate probe over what happened. Reuters reported that investigators also found unauthorized OpenAI agent communications on more than 10 previously undisclosed websites, including wikis and university link shorteners. There were also incidents involving Anthropic agents, and fears were exacerbated last week when one of the company's former researchers warned the AI race could end in human extinction . Sanders previusly warned OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta to pause AI development or face Senate action . Many Americans are moving to an anti-AI stance, whether because of fears of extinction, the building of more data centers, the automation-driven layoffs, or simply the amount of slop proliferating across the internet. But pro-AI politicians, including President Trump, say slowing AI development is a national security risk and leaves the US in a weakened position against rivals such as China. Trump recently said data center protesters are " making a mistake ." It'll certainly be interesting to see how much support Sander's legislation gains. sources.title: YouTube releases new AI features for creators within its Studio app
passages: The draft-feedback feature uses AI to look at a creator’s unpublished video and provide suggestions about pacing, structure, and storytelling.
YouTube is also debuting a new research feed in the Studio app that shows creators what kind of content is working on the platform, so they can apply their own take on it.
YouTube said creators have used its A/B testing feature to run more than 40 million tests on titles and thumbnails.
Soon, the company said, users will be able to test up to three video cuts to see which opening hook works best.
Later this year, YouTube Studio will also automatically monitor thumbnail performance and change one proactively if it doesn’t perform well.

At its Made On YouTube annual event, YouTube announced new tools for YouTube Studio, the app creators use to manage their channels, aimed at helping them analyze their videos and grow their audiences.
The updates include expanding Ask Studio, its AI-powered Q&A feature, to iOS and Android, as well as new features that provide feedback on drafts and create dynamic thumbnails.
Creators can also use a new dynamic thumbnail feature to generate three options and show each one to a different segment of their audience.
YouTube also said it’s updating its analytics to go beyond raw numbers, explaining why videos perform the way they do and providing advice about how to make content more engaging.

extraction.body: YouTube just announced a flurry of new AI-powered features for creators. But as the platform leans deeper into AI, could it impact perceptions of their authenticity and the originality of their work? On Wednesday, at the company's annual Made on YouTube event, the platform announced several new features that use generative AI. The company is revamping its Inspiration Tab in YouTube Studio, adding a new brainstorming tool to help curate video ideas, titles, thumbnails, and outlines. The feature can generate ideas based on a creator's content catalog, comments on their YouTube videos, or videos made by other creators. Creator startup Spotter recently launched a similar tool for AI-generated video ideas. YouTube is also launching AI comment replies, which will generate recommended replies to comments left under a creator's video. These tools are still under testing, and the company said it aims to launch them more widely in the coming months. The features could make it easier for creators to come up with video ideas and respond to comments faster. But will it make their activities on YouTube feel less personal and original? Many creators speak often about how important authenticity and fan connections are to their businesses. Leaning too far into AI could risk those key pillars of the creator economy. Gen AI tech is a mixed bag for YouTube and other creator-focused companies. While influencers are hungry for more tools to make video creation simpler, they're also wary of the possibility that AI-generated content could ultimately cut into their businesses. Some YouTubers are also concerned that their content has been used to train AI models without providing appropriate compensation. "Everything we build is really about enhancing that human creativity," said Neal Mohan, CEO of YouTube, during a Q&A after the Made on YouTube event. "In all the examples, hopefully, you saw that everything we show with AI was meant to enhance the work that you do. AI is foundational to how YouTube works." Mohan cited YouTube's copyright-protection tool Content ID as an example of how the company has long focused on the protection of copyright across YouTube. "You've seen us be very intentful and sometimes cautious and sometimes getting accused of overly cautious about how we bring these technologies to market," Mohan said. I think my view is that this is really what the name says: it's a tool. It's truly about streamlining some of that process, maybe giving you a couple of ideas that you may not have thought of." The company is also integrating Google DeepMind's video generation tool Veo into shorts, letting creators generate 6-second AI-generated videos for their posts.

sources.title: Is YouTube Studio Down? Issues Persist March 30 2026 as Creators Report Analytics and App Glitches
passages: YouTube Studio, the essential dashboard for millions of content creators worldwide, faced scattered access problems and functionality glitches on Monday, March 30, 2026, with users reporting difficulties viewing analytics, subscriber counts and loading certain sections of the mobile app and web interface.As of early afternoon Pacific time, multiple creators took to social media platforms including X to complain that the YouTube Studio app displayed incomplete data, error messages or failed to load tabs properly.

In previous cases, such as the global YouTube disruption on February 17, 2026, the platform attributed problems to backend systems including recommendation algorithms before confirming resolutions within hours.Creators rely heavily on YouTube Studio for daily operations.

Web access to studio.youtube.com showed mixed results, with some creators able to log in normally while others encountered loading delays or missing real-time statistics.This latest round of complaints follows a pattern of YouTube Studio instability earlier in 2026.
Similar glitches were reported in isolated Reddit threads and creator communities in mid-March.YouTube has not issued an official statement specifically addressing Monday's reports as of press time.

For smaller channels and full-time creators, even brief outages can create stress, especially when real-time analytics are unavailable during peak viewing hours.Monday's issues appeared less severe than the March 10 event, which affected loading across both mobile and desktop for many users simultaneously.

Geographic distribution of complaints suggested possible regional variations, though a clear pattern was not immediately evident.YouTube, owned by Google, has expanded its creator tools significantly in recent years to support the platform's more than 2.5 billion monthly users and millions of active channels.

A few shared screenshots showing missing analytics or error screens, urging YouTube to improve communication during technical difficulties.For those unable to access Studio, alternative methods include using third-party analytics tools (where compliant with YouTube's terms) or waiting for mobile app updates.

YouTube periodically rolls out updates to the Studio app that can temporarily introduce or resolve bugs.Looking ahead, industry analysts expect continued enhancements to creator tools, including deeper AI integration for content optimization and monetization insights.
Common issues included subscriber numbers showing as a dash or zero, analytics pages not updating, and generic "something went wrong" prompts when navigating between sections.
On March 10, the platform experienced a widespread partial outage that prevented many creators from accessing their dashboards, triggering panic among some who feared channel termination notices.
YouTube later confirmed the issue was fixed, restoring normal access and accurate statistics.
YouTube's massive scale — processing billions of hours of video daily — makes maintaining 100% uptime a complex engineering challenge.Creators offered mixed reactions online.

While the main YouTube platform for viewers appeared largely unaffected, the creator tools that allow uploading, editing metadata, checking performance and managing channels experienced intermittent disruptions.Downdetector and other outage-tracking sites showed a modest uptick in reports for YouTube-related problems, though not at the scale of major past outages.

However, when core backend services are involved, these steps offer only limited relief.YouTube has invested heavily in creator support infrastructure, including the YouTube Partner Program, dedicated help centers and community forums.
Some expressed frustration at recurring glitches, while others noted that such issues have become somewhat routine and usually resolve quickly.

While not rising to the level of major past outages, the reports highlight ongoing challenges in delivering reliable tools to a global creator base that depends on them for livelihood and audience engagement.As the day progressed, some users noted gradual improvement, with analytics beginning to load or subscriber counts reappearing.

Any disruption draws swift attention because it directly impacts income for those monetizing through ads, memberships, Super Chats and merchandise.Industry observers note that YouTube's rapid feature rollout and heavy reliance on machine learning systems can occasionally lead to backend strain.

Even short disruptions can cascade into lost opportunities, particularly for live streamers or those timing content releases around trending topics.As of Monday afternoon, no widespread confirmation of a full outage had emerged from YouTube.

Web access to studio.youtube.com showed mixed results, with some creators able to log in normally while others encountered loading delays or missing real-time statistics.This latest round of complaints follows a pattern of YouTube Studio instability earlier in 2026.

Common issues included subscriber numbers showing as a dash or zero, analytics pages not updating, and generic "something went wrong" prompts when navigating between sections.

However, when core backend services are involved, these steps offer only limited relief.YouTube has invested heavily in creator support infrastructure, including the YouTube Partner Program, dedicated help centers and community forums.
Some expressed frustration at recurring glitches, while others noted that such issues have become somewhat routine and usually resolve quickly.

While not rising to the level of major past outages, the reports highlight ongoing challenges in delivering reliable tools to a global creator base that depends on them for livelihood and audience engagement.As the day progressed, some users noted gradual improvement, with analytics beginning to load or subscriber counts reappearing.

extraction.body: YouTube just announced a flurry of new AI-powered features for creators. But as the platform leans deeper into AI, could it impact perceptions of their authenticity and the originality of their work? On Wednesday, at the company's annual Made on YouTube event, the platform announced several new features that use generative AI. The company is revamping its Inspiration Tab in YouTube Studio, adding a new brainstorming tool to help curate video ideas, titles, thumbnails, and outlines. The feature can generate ideas based on a creator's content catalog, comments on their YouTube videos, or videos made by other creators. Creator startup Spotter recently launched a similar tool for AI-generated video ideas. YouTube is also launching AI comment replies, which will generate recommended replies to comments left under a creator's video. These tools are still under testing, and the company said it aims to launch them more widely in the coming months. The features could make it easier for creators to come up with video ideas and respond to comments faster. But will it make their activities on YouTube feel less personal and original? Many creators speak often about how important authenticity and fan connections are to their businesses. Leaning too far into AI could risk those key pillars of the creator economy. Gen AI tech is a mixed bag for YouTube and other creator-focused companies. While influencers are hungry for more tools to make video creation simpler, they're also wary of the possibility that AI-generated content could ultimately cut into their businesses. Some YouTubers are also concerned that their content has been used to train AI models without providing appropriate compensation. "Everything we build is really about enhancing that human creativity," said Neal Mohan, CEO of YouTube, during a Q&A after the Made on YouTube event. "In all the examples, hopefully, you saw that everything we show with AI was meant to enhance the work that you do. AI is foundational to how YouTube works." Mohan cited YouTube's copyright-protection tool Content ID as an example of how the company has long focused on the protection of copyright across YouTube. "You've seen us be very intentful and sometimes cautious and sometimes getting accused of overly cautious about how we bring these technologies to market," Mohan said. I think my view is that this is really what the name says: it's a tool. It's truly about streamlining some of that process, maybe giving you a couple of ideas that you may not have thought of." The company is also integrating Google DeepMind's video generation tool Veo into shorts, letting creators generate 6-second AI-generated videos for their posts.

sources.title: Is YouTube Studio Down? Issues Persist March 30 2026 as Creators Report Analytics and App Glitches
passages: YouTube Studio, the essential dashboard for millions of content creators worldwide, faced scattered access problems and functionality glitches on Monday, March 30, 2026, with users reporting difficulties viewing analytics, subscriber counts and loading certain sections of the mobile app and web interface.As of early afternoon Pacific time, multiple creators took to social media platforms including X to complain that the YouTube Studio app displayed incomplete data, error messages or failed to load tabs properly.

In previous cases, such as the global YouTube disruption on February 17, 2026, the platform attributed problems to backend systems including recommendation algorithms before confirming resolutions within hours.Creators rely heavily on YouTube Studio for daily operations.

Web access to studio.youtube.com showed mixed results, with some creators able to log in normally while others encountered loading delays or missing real-time statistics.This latest round of complaints follows a pattern of YouTube Studio instability earlier in 2026.
Similar glitches were reported in isolated Reddit threads and creator communities in mid-March.YouTube has not issued an official statement specifically addressing Monday's reports as of press time.

For smaller channels and full-time creators, even brief outages can create stress, especially when real-time analytics are unavailable during peak viewing hours.Monday's issues appeared less severe than the March 10 event, which affected loading across both mobile and desktop for many users simultaneously.

Geographic distribution of complaints suggested possible regional variations, though a clear pattern was not immediately evident.YouTube, owned by Google, has expanded its creator tools significantly in recent years to support the platform's more than 2.5 billion monthly users and millions of active channels.

A few shared screenshots showing missing analytics or error screens, urging YouTube to improve communication during technical difficulties.For those unable to access Studio, alternative methods include using third-party analytics tools (where compliant with YouTube's terms) or waiting for mobile app updates.

YouTube periodically rolls out updates to the Studio app that can temporarily introduce or resolve bugs.Looking ahead, industry analysts expect continued enhancements to creator tools, including deeper AI integration for content optimization and monetization insights.
Common issues included subscriber numbers showing as a dash or zero, analytics pages not updating, and generic "something went wrong" prompts when navigating between sections.
On March 10, the platform experienced a widespread partial outage that prevented many creators from accessing their dashboards, triggering panic among some who feared channel termination notices.
YouTube later confirmed the issue was fixed, restoring normal access and accurate statistics.
YouTube's massive scale — processing billions of hours of video daily — makes maintaining 100% uptime a complex engineering challenge.Creators offered mixed reactions online.

While the main YouTube platform for viewers appeared largely unaffected, the creator tools that allow uploading, editing metadata, checking performance and managing channels experienced intermittent disruptions.Downdetector and other outage-tracking sites showed a modest uptick in reports for YouTube-related problems, though not at the scale of major past outages.

However, when core backend services are involved, these steps offer only limited relief.YouTube has invested heavily in creator support infrastructure, including the YouTube Partner Program, dedicated help centers and community forums.
Some expressed frustration at recurring glitches, while others noted that such issues have become somewhat routine and usually resolve quickly.

While not rising to the level of major past outages, the reports highlight ongoing challenges in delivering reliable tools to a global creator base that depends on them for livelihood and audience engagement.As the day progressed, some users noted gradual improvement, with analytics beginning to load or subscriber counts reappearing.

Any disruption draws swift attention because it directly impacts income for those monetizing through ads, memberships, Super Chats and merchandise.Industry observers note that YouTube's rapid feature rollout and heavy reliance on machine learning systems can occasionally lead to backend strain.

Even short disruptions can cascade into lost opportunities, particularly for live streamers or those timing content releases around trending topics.As of Monday afternoon, no widespread confirmation of a full outage had emerged from YouTube.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump says he is banning three major news outlets, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, from the White House due to what he called "unfavorable coverage." Trump didn't provide details on how the ban would be implemented, but warned he might bar other media outlets as well. White House Correspondent Liz Landers reports on the administration's latest test of First Amendment protections. Geoff Bennett: Well, President Trump today also announced he's banning three major news outlets, CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, from the White House, accusing them of reporting what he calls fake news. In a social media post, the president said -- quote -- "Media outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report fiction and lies." And he suggested other news organizations could face similar action. Trump said this: President Donald Trump: They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration. Geoff Bennett: Our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, joins us now. So, what did the president say to justify this action? Liz Landers: Well, the president admitted today that there was no particular reason why this happened today. He, of course, has gripes with the press almost all the time. He makes that very clear when he speaks publicly and also in social media posts. But he, as you mentioned, says that these news outlets write negative news, though he did not specifically say which news stories he is talking about. This is another troubling escalation from a president that has attacked the First Amendment and the free press in his first administration and now in his second one. During his first administration, he banned particular reporters, but not entire news outlets, like we're seeing today. This term, the Associated Press has been removed from the press pool, which PBS is a part of, and the White House has taken over the pool rotation. The president was asked in the Oval Office today in the afternoon when those badges were being pulled. We as White House reporters have badges that we wear. He said he didn't know, but he wants the ban to go as far as it can. He says that other outlets may be added to this list, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: And how are the outlets themselves responding to all of this? Liz Landers: CNN is still reporting from the White House, and they have also released a statement from CNN P.R. saying that they stand by their fair and accurate reporting, and they add that if this ban goes into effect, it will be "an illegal assault on constitutionally protected right to free speech." Politico said that their outlet will continue to defend their First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them. Leading press freedom groups are also reacting to this. The Freedom of the Press Foundation said in a statement -- quote -- "It's difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the people's house for criticizing the government. It's also hard to imagine a dumber move." And, Geoff, former Republican White House Press Secretary Ari Fleischer took to X to say that banning certain news outlets is not the solution to this. He said, instead, try to win the argument with reporters. So we are seeing Republicans push back on this as well. Geoff Bennett: OK, Liz Landers, thanks, as always.

A lawyer for the outlets slammed the DOJ’s position as “exceptionally weak.” A hearing in the case is slated for Wednesday afternoon. “We look forward to the hearing,” attorney Ted Boutrous told Politico. extraction.body: The Associated Press is suing members of President Trump's administration for blocking its reporters from "pool" access after it refused to use the term "Gulf of America." The suit claims that blocking AP violates the First Amendment. More specifically, the suit argues that the government's content-based restrictions on press access amount to unconstitutional control and retaliation against speech. AP has received support from various news outlets, including Fox News and Newsmax. The Associated Press (AP) is suing members of President Donald Trump’s administration. The AP's reporters were blocked from accessing the White House for refusing to use the “Gulf of America” designation ordered by the president. District Court in Washington, D.C., a little more than a week after members of the administration didn’t grant its reporters “pool” access to an executive order signing in the Oval Office. The case was assigned to Judge Trevor McFadden, who was appointed by Trump in 2017. The suit names White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, Deputy Chief of Staff Taylor Budowich and Chief of Staff Susan Wiles. “The Press and all people in the United States have the right to choose their own words and not be retaliated against by the government,” the suit states. Allowing such government control and retaliation to stand is a threat to every American’s freedom.” Trump made clear that the newswire service would be blocked from accessing pool areas until its coverage reflected his order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” “The Associated Press refuses to go with what the law is and what’s taken place. It’s called the Gulf of America now; it’s not called the Gulf of Mexico any longer,” Trump said. AP has seen support from dozens of news outlets, including Trump-friendly media organizations like Fox News and Newsmax, in asking the president to reinstate AP’s access. “We can understand President Trump’s frustration because the media has often been unfair to him, but Newsmax supports the AP’s right, as a private organization, to use the language it wants to use in its reporting,” Newsmax said in a statement. “We fear a future administration may not like something Newsmax writes and seek to ban us.” Related Stories AP says White House blocked reporter over Gulf of America policy Axios will use ‘Gulf of America’ but defends AP amid White House scrutiny Fox News, Newsmax among 40 outlets asking Trump to reinstate AP access

extraction.body: In a bid to help creators reach more people, YouTube on Wednesday unveiled a slew of new tools, many of which use AI to try out different tactics on videos to find what makes them perform best. The new Ask Studio feature allows creators to share draft videos with AI to get personalized feedback based on their previous content and user comments. The feature will propose alternative titles and thumbnail options, analyze the creator’s channel analytics to explain the performance of their videos, and offer advice for improving metrics. Ask Studio is expanding to YouTube’s mobile apps, too. YouTube already allows creators to A/B test titles and thumbnails, and from 2027, this feature will let creators upload and test three different cuts for Shorts. There’s also a Dynamic Thumbnails feature, with which creators can upload multiple thumbnails and leave it to YouTube to determine which thumbnail to show viewers that is most likely to spark their interest. Creators can also apply these tools to their existing catalog. If a creator allows it, Ask Studio will be able to autonomously monitor thumbnail performance and create tests to refine older videos. On the shopping front, YouTube will now use AI to auto-tag products, which it says will help creators earn money through affiliate programs. The company is also expanding its Amazon affiliate program beyond the U.S. Some creators are understandably skeptical of using AI to support their content, worrying that just one AI-generated mistake could harm their credibility. For such features to succeed, they will need to be accurate enough to assuage creators’ concerns. The platform is also giving creators new ways to go live. Early next year, YouTube will pilot auto-dubbing on live videos to translate creators’ speech into other languages in real time. The company is also launching a “live showdown” feature, which lets creators co-host streams together, and even get paired with other creators currently streaming through “live creator matchmaking.” “Co-hosts can kick off friendly head-to-head matchups, where viewers send chats, gifts, and Super Chats to push their creator’s score forward on-screen in real time,” YouTube Live product manager Barbara MacDonald wrote in a blog post . Hopefully these impromptu collaborations with strangers won’t turn into a hotbed of bad behavior. YouTube also shared data that provides insight into how people are using the platform. More people continue to watch YouTube on household TVs , and more than half of the top 100 YouTube creators have “living room” as their most watched interface. YouTube’s data also confirms what we know about the growth of the microdrama industry : In the first half of 2026, microdramas on YouTube surpassed 6.5 billion views, and their watch time rose 50% year-over-year. People even seem to be watching these episodic, vertical video series on the big screen, with views of microdrama content on TVs increasing 90% year-over-year. If you’ve tuned into previous editions of YouTube’s product spiel, the headlines for the 2026 presentation may sound familiar. YouTube is bringing more AI-powered personalization to both creators and viewers, and new testing tools will optimize the platform’s videos across multiple formats. Creators are always looking for any slight advantage that can make their content stand out amid a noisy field. YouTube Studio is delivering that optimization in multiple ways. “YouTube Studio is evolving into an end-to-end creative partner to help across production, packaging, and channel strategy,” reads a Made On blog post attributed to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan . For starters, the platform is expanding the A/B tests it has been slowly introducing since 2023. Those experiments already allow creators to pit multiple titles and thumbnails against each other to determine which one performs better. Soon, that process will expand to entire videos. By A/B testing multiple cuts of the same clip, creators can identify the version that best resonates with their audience. Those tests can locate what YouTube calls “outlier videos”: exceptional performers that can inspire future uploads. New Insights and Research data in YouTube Studio can add more context to those outliers, and the same philosophy is being applied to thumbnails, too. After bringing dynamic insertion to its ads at last year’s Made On event, YouTube is now introducing dynamic thumbnails. By automatically switching between multiple preview images, YouTube is aiming to maximize reach among specific audience segments. As part of its Made On pitch, YouTbe alluded to its first-ever GenAI trends report , which found that 72% of U.S. video uploaders between the ages of 14 and 44 have used AI as a creative aid over the past year. AI suggestions delivered by Google’s Gemini models are saving time for users while turning YouTube into a more targeted experience. If you think AI-powered personalization is already ubiquitous on YouTube, just wait. As we learned at Made On, YouTube is finding more ways to tailor its design to individual users. For social shoppers, an expanded Ask YouTube feature will turn questions and follow-ups into interactive product recommendations that show up across TV and mobile surfaces. And to improve a destination Mohan called “the #1 podcast platform for viewers in the US,” YouTube is building personalized podcast lineups that reflect each listener’s tastes and interests. A similar mechanism is coming to YouTube’s homepage. At Made On, Mohan officially announced the new Custom Feeds . That tool can turn users’ suggestions into fully populated landing pages that cut across specific content categories. “Custom Feeds allows you to create dedicated tabs for any interest, routine, or mood,” said video essayist Mina Le at the Made On event. “Just prompt a new feed into existence and it appears right there on your homepage, constantly updating with hyper-relevant creators and content.” In other words, YouTube homepage shelves will now deliver the granular recommendations Netflix users have come to expect. But YouTube’s copycat approach doesn’t stop there. Made On YouTube 2026 shows that Mohan and his deputies are paying attention to the formats, features, and products that are shining on other platforms. A lot of that has to do with AI; YouTube, like Spotify, wants to automate audio recommendations, which is why it’s bringing Ask Music — its version of the Spotify DJ — to the YouTube Music app. When it comes to TikTok, however, YouTube is borrowing much more than just AI-powered updates. It is leaning into the growing popularity of microdramas by expanding its Series feature . TikTok has found ways to monetize serialized short-form collections , and YouTube is taking a step in that direction with the introduction of Shorts Series . The sequential short-form playlists will build on YouTube’s current microdrama momentum, which includes more than six billion views . Then, there’s the matter of TikTok LIVE, a popular vertical live-streaming format that has inspired Made On YouTube updates over the past three years. To make its own Vertical Live streams as functional as their TikTok analogues, YouTube is introducing several new broadcast options. Go Live Together will enable co-hosting on those streams, Live showdowns will turn them into collaborative fundraisers, and Live auto-dubbing will bring streaming content to viewers across the globe. All of those Vertical Live updates are due to arrive in “early 2027.” From that point on, YouTube has no plans to slow down. Instead, users can expect the flurry of new features to continue. “Since the start of the year, we’ve launched over 3,000 product updates and improvements, keeping up with evolving viewer tastes and increasing creator ambitions,” Mohan said at Made On. “This is what it looks like to innovate in the YouTube era.” Stay up-to-date with the latest and breaking creator and online video news delivered right to your inbox.

passages: The $100 billion creator payout milestone represents approximately 45% of YouTube's total advertising revenue over the four-year period, according to industry estimates.
This revenue sharing rate significantly exceeds traditional media industry standards where content creators typically receive 10-15% of advertising revenue.
YouTube unveiled its largest creator features update at Made on YouTube 2025, introducing AI-powered content creation tools and marking $100 billion paid to creators over four years.
YouTube Partner Program membership reached 3 million channels, with 700,000 joining over the past three years.
Gross Merchandise Volume through YouTube Shopping grew 5X year-over-year with over 500,000 creators enrolled globally as of July 2025.
The integration of Veo 3 Fast represents significant computational requirements for YouTube's infrastructure.
According to technical documentation, the system processes text prompts through Google DeepMind's neural networks while maintaining 480p output resolution to balance quality with processing speed.
The reduced latency design enables real-time content generation on mobile devices, requiring substantial backend optimization.
The announcement represents significant developments for digital marketing strategies, particularly regarding creator partnerships and video advertising.
PPC Land has extensively covered YouTube's expanding role in the creator economy , noting the platform's evolution from simple video hosting to comprehensive business infrastructure.
Other features deploy across all YouTube markets with varying timelines.
This marks the first time creators can generate video content with sound from text prompts directly within the platform.
The feature launches initially in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, with expansion planned for additional markets.
Creator economy growth impacts traditional advertising agency models as brands increasingly allocate budgets toward creator partnerships rather than conventional media placements.
PPC Land analysis shows creator content marketing receives 89% advertiser approval , with 44% of marketers planning investment increases.
Enhanced targeting capabilities in YouTube Shopping align with broader programmatic advertising trends.
TikTok's Effect House and Instagram's AR tools provide comparable creation features, but lack the integrated monetization infrastructure YouTube offers through its Partner Program.
The combination of AI content creation with established revenue sharing creates competitive advantages for creator retention and platform loyalty.
This tool converts dialogue from eligible videos into musical soundtracks for Shorts.

Meta's Reels platform competes directly in short-form video content but relies primarily on external AI tools rather than integrated generation capabilities.

Over 30% of daily logged-in viewers watched live content in Q2 2025 according to platform statistics.
New features include simultaneous horizontal and vertical streaming with unified chat, practice mode for new streamers, and AI-powered highlight extraction for Shorts creation.
The dynamic brand segment insertion feature addresses advertiser demands for campaign flexibility that competing platforms struggle to match.
Traditional social media sponsorships require permanent content integration, while YouTube's system enables post-publication modifications and market-specific targeting.
Creators can ask questions like "catch me up on how my last video is performing" or "tell me what my community is saying about my editing style."

The system analyzes facial movements, speech patterns, and timing across 20 languages while maintaining natural appearance. Processing requirements increase substantially when combining voice generation with visual lip synchronization compared to audio-only translation.

The combination of AI content creation with established revenue sharing creates competitive advantages for creator retention and platform loyalty.

YouTube's approach embeds creation tools within the platform ecosystem, reducing friction for creators who previously required separate applications or services.

Traditional social media sponsorships require permanent content integration, while YouTube's system enables post-publication modifications and market-specific targeting.

The $100 billion creator payout milestone represents approximately 45% of YouTube's total advertising revenue over the four-year period, according to industry estimates. Creator economy growth impacts traditional advertising agency models as brands increasingly allocate budgets toward creator partnerships rather than conventional media placements. PPC Land analysis shows creator content marketing receives 89% advertiser approval , with 44% of marketers planning investment increases.

The platform's creator economy expansion may reach saturation points where increased creator numbers dilute individual earning potential. YouTube's growth strategy depends on expanding total advertising revenue faster than creator population growth to maintain attractive monetization rates.

The announcement represents significant developments for digital marketing strategies, particularly regarding creator partnerships and video advertising. PPC Land has extensively covered YouTube's expanding role in the creator economy , noting the platform's evolution from simple video hosting to comprehensive business infrastructure.

The AI-powered content creation tools could democratize high-quality video production, potentially increasing competition in creator marketing spaces. The collaboration features could impact influencer marketing campaign planning by enabling multi-creator partnerships with clearer attribution models. Brands working with creator collectives or campaign series can better track performance across participant channels while maintaining unified campaign messaging.

extraction.body: YouTube is giving creators more tools to test, optimize and distribute their content as the platform expands its use of artificial intelligence across video creation and discovery. The company announced a series of new creator features on Wednesday, including AI-powered feedback through Ask Studio, video A/B testing, dynamic thumbnails, automated product tagging and real-time dubbing for live videos. The tools are designed to help creators understand what works on their channels, improve existing videos and reach audiences in more markets. YouTube is expanding Ask Studio, its AI assistant for creators, to mobile apps. The tool can analyse draft videos and provide personalised feedback based on a creator’s previous content and audience comments. It can also suggest alternative titles and thumbnails while analysing channel analytics to explain why particular videos performed the way they did. Ask Studio can then offer recommendations on how creators could improve their content and performance. YouTube is also extending some of these capabilities to older videos. With a creator’s permission, Ask Studio can monitor thumbnail performance and automatically create tests to determine whether different thumbnails improve how viewers respond to existing content. YouTube already allows creators to test different titles and thumbnails to determine which versions perform better. The company plans to expand this capability in 2027 by allowing creators to upload and test up to three different cuts of a Short. The platform is also introducing Dynamic Thumbnails , which allows creators to upload multiple thumbnails and lets YouTube determine which one to show to viewers based on which is most likely to generate interest. The feature could reduce the need for creators to manually monitor thumbnail performance and repeatedly change thumbnails based on analytics. However, the increased use of AI in content optimisation also raises concerns among creators who worry that inaccurate AI-generated suggestions could affect their credibility or misrepresent their content. For these tools to gain wider adoption, creators will need to trust that the recommendations and automated changes are accurate and aligned with their content. YouTube is also using AI to make video shopping easier for creators. The platform will automatically identify and tag products featured in videos, helping creators connect their content to affiliate opportunities and potentially earn commissions from product sales. YouTube is also expanding its Amazon affiliate programme beyond the United States. The changes come as the platform increasingly connects video discovery with shopping, allowing creators to turn product-focused content into another source of revenue. YouTube is expanding its live-streaming tools with features aimed at helping creators reach audiences beyond their primary language. Early next year, the platform plans to pilot automatic dubbing for live videos. The technology will translate a creator’s speech into other languages in real time, allowing viewers in different markets to follow live content in their own language. Real-time dubbing could make live streams more accessible internationally while allowing creators to reach audiences without having to produce separate versions of their content. The company is also launching a feature called Live Showdown , which will allow creators to co-host streams and compete against each other in real time. A related live creator matchmaking feature will pair creators with other creators who are currently streaming, creating opportunities for spontaneous collaborations. During a Live Showdown, viewers can support their preferred creator through chats, gifts and Super Chats, with the creator’s score displayed on screen in real time. The format gives YouTube another way to make live content more interactive while encouraging collaborations between creators. YouTube also shared new data showing how viewing habits are changing on the platform. More viewers are watching YouTube through household televisions, with more than half of the platform’s top 100 creators having the living room as their most-watched viewing interface. Short-form episodic content is also gaining traction. Microdramas generated more than 6.5 billion views on YouTube during the first half of 2026 , while watch time for the format increased 50% year over year. The growth is not limited to mobile devices. Views of microdrama content on televisions increased 90% year over year, suggesting that audiences are increasingly consuming vertical, episodic content on larger screens. The new features show YouTube’s broader effort to integrate AI into different stages of the creator experience, from developing content and choosing thumbnails to analysing performance, monetising videos and reaching international audiences. For creators, the tools could reduce some of the manual work involved in optimising a channel. But their success will also depend on whether creators trust AI to make recommendations and automated decisions without compromising the quality or authenticity of their content. As YouTube continues to expand beyond traditional video recommendations, the platform is positioning AI as a central part of how creators produce, optimise, distribute and monetise their work.

extraction.body: In a bid to help creators reach more people, YouTube on Wednesday unveiled a slew of new tools, many of which use AI to try out different tactics on videos to find what makes them perform best. The new Ask Studio feature allows creators to share draft videos with AI to get personalized feedback based on their previous content and user comments. The feature will propose alternative titles and thumbnail options, analyze the creator’s channel analytics to explain the performance of their videos, and offer advice for improving metrics. Ask Studio is expanding to YouTube’s mobile apps, too. YouTube already allows creators to A/B test titles and thumbnails, and from 2027, this feature will let creators upload and test three different cuts for Shorts. There’s also a Dynamic Thumbnails feature, with which creators can upload multiple thumbnails and leave it to YouTube to determine which thumbnail to show viewers that is most likely to spark their interest. Creators can also apply these tools to their existing catalog. If a creator allows it, Ask Studio will be able to autonomously monitor thumbnail performance and create tests to refine older videos. On the shopping front, YouTube will now use AI to auto-tag products, which it says will help creators earn money through affiliate programs. The company is also expanding its Amazon affiliate program beyond the U.S. Some creators are understandably skeptical of using AI to support their content, worrying that just one AI-generated mistake could harm their credibility. For such features to succeed, they will need to be accurate enough to assuage creators’ concerns. The platform is also giving creators new ways to go live. Early next year, YouTube will pilot auto-dubbing on live videos to translate creators’ speech into other languages in real time. The company is also launching a “live showdown” feature, which lets creators co-host streams together, and even get paired with other creators currently streaming through “live creator matchmaking.” “Co-hosts can kick off friendly head-to-head matchups, where viewers send chats, gifts, and Super Chats to push their creator’s score forward on-screen in real time,” YouTube Live product manager Barbara MacDonald wrote in a blog post . Hopefully these impromptu collaborations with strangers won’t turn into a hotbed of bad behavior. YouTube also shared data that provides insight into how people are using the platform. More people continue to watch YouTube on household TVs , and more than half of the top 100 YouTube creators have “living room” as their most watched interface. YouTube’s data also confirms what we know about the growth of the microdrama industry : In the first half of 2026, microdramas on YouTube surpassed 6.5 billion views, and their watch time rose 50% year-over-year. People even seem to be watching these episodic, vertical video series on the big screen, with views of microdrama content on TVs increasing 90% year-over-year. extraction.body: On September 23 , YouTube held its annual Made On event in New York City. If you’ve tuned into previous editions of YouTube’s product spiel, the headlines for the 2026 presentation may sound familiar. YouTube is bringing more AI-powered personalization to both creators and viewers, and new testing tools will optimize the platform’s videos across multiple formats. Creators are always looking for any slight advantage that can make their content stand out amid a noisy field. YouTube Studio is delivering that optimization in multiple ways. “YouTube Studio is evolving into an end-to-end creative partner to help across production, packaging, and channel strategy,” reads a Made On blog post attributed to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan . For starters, the platform is expanding the A/B tests it has been slowly introducing since 2023. Those experiments already allow creators to pit multiple titles and thumbnails against each other to determine which one performs better. Soon, that process will expand to entire videos. By A/B testing multiple cuts of the same clip, creators can identify the version that best resonates with their audience. Those tests can locate what YouTube calls “outlier videos”: exceptional performers that can inspire future uploads. New Insights and Research data in YouTube Studio can add more context to those outliers, and the same philosophy is being applied to thumbnails, too. After bringing dynamic insertion to its ads at last year’s Made On event, YouTube is now introducing dynamic thumbnails. By automatically switching between multiple preview images, YouTube is aiming to maximize reach among specific audience segments. As part of its Made On pitch, YouTbe alluded to its first-ever GenAI trends report , which found that 72% of U.S. video uploaders between the ages of 14 and 44 have used AI as a creative aid over the past year. AI suggestions delivered by Google’s Gemini models are saving time for users while turning YouTube into a more targeted experience. If you think AI-powered personalization is already ubiquitous on YouTube, just wait. As we learned at Made On, YouTube is finding more ways to tailor its design to individual users. For social shoppers, an expanded Ask YouTube feature will turn questions and follow-ups into interactive product recommendations that show up across TV and mobile surfaces. And to improve a destination Mohan called “the #1 podcast platform for viewers in the US,” YouTube is building personalized podcast lineups that reflect each listener’s tastes and interests. A similar mechanism is coming to YouTube’s homepage. At Made On, Mohan officially announced the new Custom Feeds . That tool can turn users’ suggestions into fully populated landing pages that cut across specific content categories. “Custom Feeds allows you to create dedicated tabs for any interest, routine, or mood,” said video essayist Mina Le at the Made On event. “Just prompt a new feed into existence and it appears right there on your homepage, constantly updating with hyper-relevant creators and content.” In other words, YouTube homepage shelves will now deliver the granular recommendations Netflix users have come to expect. But YouTube’s copycat approach doesn’t stop there. Made On YouTube 2026 shows that Mohan and his deputies are paying attention to the formats, features, and products that are shining on other platforms. A lot of that has to do with AI; YouTube, like Spotify, wants to automate audio recommendations, which is why it’s bringing Ask Music — its version of the Spotify DJ — to the YouTube Music app. When it comes to TikTok, however, YouTube is borrowing much more than just AI-powered updates. It is leaning into the growing popularity of microdramas by expanding its Series feature . TikTok has found ways to monetize serialized short-form collections , and YouTube is taking a step in that direction with the introduction of Shorts Series . The sequential short-form playlists will build on YouTube’s current microdrama momentum, which includes more than six billion views . Then, there’s the matter of TikTok LIVE, a popular vertical live-streaming format that has inspired Made On YouTube updates over the past three years. To make its own Vertical Live streams as functional as their TikTok analogues, YouTube is introducing several new broadcast options. Go Live Together will enable co-hosting on those streams, Live showdowns will turn them into collaborative fundraisers, and Live auto-dubbing will bring streaming content to viewers across the globe. All of those Vertical Live updates are due to arrive in “early 2027.” From that point on, YouTube has no plans to slow down. Instead, users can expect the flurry of new features to continue. “Since the start of the year, we’ve launched over 3,000 product updates and improvements, keeping up with evolving viewer tastes and increasing creator ambitions,” Mohan said at Made On. “This is what it looks like to innovate in the YouTube era.” Stay up-to-date with the latest and breaking creator and online video news delivered right to your inbox.

Other features deploy across all YouTube markets with varying timelines.

Enhanced targeting capabilities in YouTube Shopping align with broader programmatic advertising trends.
TikTok's Effect House and Instagram's AR tools provide comparable creation features, but lack the integrated monetization infrastructure YouTube offers through its Partner Program.
The combination of AI content creation with established revenue sharing creates competitive advantages for creator retention and platform loyalty.

Traditional social media sponsorships require permanent content integration, while YouTube's system enables post-publication modifications and market-specific targeting.

extraction.body: YouTube is giving creators more tools to test, optimize and distribute their content as the platform expands its use of artificial intelligence across video creation and discovery. The company announced a series of new creator features on Wednesday, including AI-powered feedback through Ask Studio, video A/B testing, dynamic thumbnails, automated product tagging and real-time dubbing for live videos. The tools are designed to help creators understand what works on their channels, improve existing videos and reach audiences in more markets. YouTube is expanding Ask Studio, its AI assistant for creators, to mobile apps. The tool can analyse draft videos and provide personalised feedback based on a creator’s previous content and audience comments. It can also suggest alternative titles and thumbnails while analysing channel analytics to explain why particular videos performed the way they did. Ask Studio can then offer recommendations on how creators could improve their content and performance. YouTube is also extending some of these capabilities to older videos. With a creator’s permission, Ask Studio can monitor thumbnail performance and automatically create tests to determine whether different thumbnails improve how viewers respond to existing content. YouTube already allows creators to test different titles and thumbnails to determine which versions perform better. The company plans to expand this capability in 2027 by allowing creators to upload and test up to three different cuts of a Short. The platform is also introducing Dynamic Thumbnails , which allows creators to upload multiple thumbnails and lets YouTube determine which one to show to viewers based on which is most likely to generate interest. The feature could reduce the need for creators to manually monitor thumbnail performance and repeatedly change thumbnails based on analytics. However, the increased use of AI in content optimisation also raises concerns among creators who worry that inaccurate AI-generated suggestions could affect their credibility or misrepresent their content. For these tools to gain wider adoption, creators will need to trust that the recommendations and automated changes are accurate and aligned with their content. YouTube is also using AI to make video shopping easier for creators. The platform will automatically identify and tag products featured in videos, helping creators connect their content to affiliate opportunities and potentially earn commissions from product sales. YouTube is also expanding its Amazon affiliate programme beyond the United States. The changes come as the platform increasingly connects video discovery with shopping, allowing creators to turn product-focused content into another source of revenue. YouTube is expanding its live-streaming tools with features aimed at helping creators reach audiences beyond their primary language. Early next year, the platform plans to pilot automatic dubbing for live videos. The technology will translate a creator’s speech into other languages in real time, allowing viewers in different markets to follow live content in their own language. Real-time dubbing could make live streams more accessible internationally while allowing creators to reach audiences without having to produce separate versions of their content. The company is also launching a feature called Live Showdown , which will allow creators to co-host streams and compete against each other in real time. A related live creator matchmaking feature will pair creators with other creators who are currently streaming, creating opportunities for spontaneous collaborations. During a Live Showdown, viewers can support their preferred creator through chats, gifts and Super Chats, with the creator’s score displayed on screen in real time. The format gives YouTube another way to make live content more interactive while encouraging collaborations between creators. YouTube also shared new data showing how viewing habits are changing on the platform. More viewers are watching YouTube through household televisions, with more than half of the platform’s top 100 creators having the living room as their most-watched viewing interface. Short-form episodic content is also gaining traction. Microdramas generated more than 6.5 billion views on YouTube during the first half of 2026 , while watch time for the format increased 50% year over year. The growth is not limited to mobile devices. Views of microdrama content on televisions increased 90% year over year, suggesting that audiences are increasingly consuming vertical, episodic content on larger screens. The new features show YouTube’s broader effort to integrate AI into different stages of the creator experience, from developing content and choosing thumbnails to analysing performance, monetising videos and reaching international audiences. For creators, the tools could reduce some of the manual work involved in optimising a channel. But their success will also depend on whether creators trust AI to make recommendations and automated decisions without compromising the quality or authenticity of their content. As YouTube continues to expand beyond traditional video recommendations, the platform is positioning AI as a central part of how creators produce, optimise, distribute and monetise their work.

extraction.body: Part of the job of a content creator is to figure out how to get their work in front of the most people. Cracking — or fighting — the algorithm has historically been a frustration for creators, but YouTube is increasingly simply telling creators what they should do. At the annual creator-focused Made on YouTube event, the company announced updates to the suite of AI-powered creator tools it unveiled in 2025. In its initial iteration, the dashboard of creator tools included things like A/B testing for video thumbnails and a chatbot interface to query how content was performing. This year’s update adds AI tools for more complex tasks. Perhaps most significantly, YouTube is introducing an AI “agent” that will work in the background to optimize a creator’s channel. For example, the tool will monitor a creator’s back catalog of videos, looking for content that has taken on a new life, is relevant to the news, or has started trending. The agent will offer suggestions for tweaking the thumbnails or titles for older videos to ride the new wave of relevance. The agent will now generate entire thumbnails and titles based on the content of an uploaded video, and creators can ask the tool for feedback on their own thumbnails. Viewers may also see different content as creators run tests via YouTube Studio: A dynamic thumbnail tool allows creators to upload up to three different images for each video, and YouTube’s system will assign the best one to different audience segments to try to boost watch time. YouTube is taking it a step further, too, by allowing creators to test three different versions of videos — a clip with a different intro and hook, for example, or with a different structure — to see how each performs. The different versions of the same video will be fed to small audience segments to test which results in the highest watch time; creators can go forward with the “winner” to make it the permanent video, or YouTube will automatically do so after seven days. Hanif says the YouTube system ensures the three video versions are not “dramatically different” from one another. Earlier this summer, Hank Green angered fans when he acknowledged that he had been relying on AI to do research for his videos. (Some observers diagnosed Green’s problem as not one specifically about AI, but rather about overwork and burnout in the creator industry.) It’s not just Green who’s had to defend himself: There are countless stories of brands using or promoting AI — or simply being suspected of doing so — that have spiraled into scandal. For many content creators or public figures, using AI in their work is a reputational risk; is using YouTube’s behind-the-scenes AI tools something they’re worried about? Hanif differentiates between instances where creators are using AI to be more efficient, versus when the tools are doing the actual job of a creator. “What I’ve heard from creators and what I’ve seen from my own conversations with viewers is that when it feels like it’s not actually from the creator, but the tools have taken over and the tools are producing the content, I think that’s kind of where it crosses the line a bit,” Hanif says. Writing the script, shooting the scenes, wholesale creating the content — these are the types of AI use that might become a problem for creators and viewers, he says. The real question is what tangible effects this suite of AI tools actually has on creator success. Does using the chatbot to plan or tweak content help creators connect more with what their audiences want to see? I asked YouTube and Hanif if they had data that shows the tools actually improving metrics for the creators who use them, but the company declined to share anything. “The time that we’ve saved there is time that goes back into the creativity,” Hanif says.

Cracking — or fighting — the algorithm has historically been a frustration for creators, but YouTube is increasingly simply telling creators what they should do.

YouTube is taking it a step further, too, by allowing creators to test three different versions of videos — a clip with a different intro and hook, for example, or with a different structure — to see how each performs.
For many content creators or public figures, using AI in their work is a reputational risk; is using YouTube’s behind-the-scenes AI tools something they’re worried about?
In its initial iteration, the dashboard of creator tools included things like A/B testing for video thumbnails and a chatbot interface to query how content was performing.
Hanif says the YouTube system ensures the three video versions are not “dramatically different” from one another.
Hanif differentiates between instances where creators are using AI to be more efficient, versus when the tools are doing the actual job of a creator.

Sometimes I remove people from the shots or just expand the scene a bit more to fit a more suitable aspect ratio.” This is a family that loves and has fun with what they do. passages: There is a subtle revolution unfolding across India’s digital landscape and it is not led by corporations or legacy media but by Gen Z, the 18–24-year-olds who are rewriting what it means to “make content.” According to a 2024 YouTube India–SmithGeiger report, a staggering 83% of Indian Gen Zers consider themselves creators.
Gen Z in India is treating content creation as real work.
Over 90% of Gen Z creators in the report use YouTube to express their ideas, talents or knowledge.

The implications are huge:A more democratic creator economyA renaissance of regional contentYouth entrepreneurship powered by passion, not just pay checksDigital spaces as platforms for social changeIn the end: The creator dream is realThe next time you scroll through YouTube or watch a video in your local language, remember that the person behind that content is likely part of this Gen Z surge.

It is a profound shift in identity, ambition and how young Indians are forging their futures, especially in cities beyond the megacities.From tier-2 dreams to digital stardomOne of the most striking revelations of the report is about where many of these creators are coming from.
From folk music to regional fashion, they are turning corners of India into digital landmarks.The weight of responsibilityWith power comes responsibility.
In many ways, social media has flattened the opportunity.Creator is the new career: Making money, making meaningThis is not just hobby content anymore.
More than half of the creators surveyed (55%) said digital platforms helped them gain financial independence.

Shorts have been especially pivotal - quick, mobile-first and deeply rooted in the language and styles of smaller-town India.Women are rising in the creator equationThe digital wave is lifting more than just location-diverse creators as it is also lifting the voices of young women.
According to the report, the number of female creators on YouTube has risen by 40% in just the past two years.

The creator economy is no longer side hustle, it is the main hustle and for a generation that grew up online, that feels both natural and powerful.YouTube is their Canvas and their stageWhen it comes to platform choice, YouTube still dominates.
Platforms like YouTube, Instagram and Shorts are not just for fun, they are tools to build businesses, earn sponsorships and monetise passionately.
