coreStoryFacts.text: At the annual creator-focused Made on YouTube event, the company announced updates to the suite of AI-powered creator tools it unveiled in 2025.
I asked YouTube and Hanif if they had data that shows the tools actually improving metrics for the creators who use them, but the company declined to share anything.
Perhaps most significantly, YouTube is introducing an AI “agent” that will work in the background to optimize a creator’s channel.
Cracking — or fighting — the algorithm has historically been a frustration for creators, but YouTube is increasingly simply telling creators what they should do.

YouTube is taking it a step further, too, by allowing creators to test three different versions of videos — a clip with a different intro and hook, for example, or with a different structure — to see how each performs.
For many content creators or public figures, using AI in their work is a reputational risk; is using YouTube’s behind-the-scenes AI tools something they’re worried about?
In its initial iteration, the dashboard of creator tools included things like A/B testing for video thumbnails and a chatbot interface to query how content was performing.

extraction.body: Part of the job of a content creator is to figure out how to get their work in front of the most people. Cracking — or fighting — the algorithm has historically been a frustration for creators, but YouTube is increasingly simply telling creators what they should do. At the annual creator-focused Made on YouTube event, the company announced updates to the suite of AI-powered creator tools it unveiled in 2025. In its initial iteration, the dashboard of creator tools included things like A/B testing for video thumbnails and a chatbot interface to query how content was performing. This year’s update adds AI tools for more complex tasks. Perhaps most significantly, YouTube is introducing an AI “agent” that will work in the background to optimize a creator’s channel. For example, the tool will monitor a creator’s back catalog of videos, looking for content that has taken on a new life, is relevant to the news, or has started trending. The agent will offer suggestions for tweaking the thumbnails or titles for older videos to ride the new wave of relevance. The agent will now generate entire thumbnails and titles based on the content of an uploaded video, and creators can ask the tool for feedback on their own thumbnails. Viewers may also see different content as creators run tests via YouTube Studio: A dynamic thumbnail tool allows creators to upload up to three different images for each video, and YouTube’s system will assign the best one to different audience segments to try to boost watch time. YouTube is taking it a step further, too, by allowing creators to test three different versions of videos — a clip with a different intro and hook, for example, or with a different structure — to see how each performs. The different versions of the same video will be fed to small audience segments to test which results in the highest watch time; creators can go forward with the “winner” to make it the permanent video, or YouTube will automatically do so after seven days. Hanif says the YouTube system ensures the three video versions are not “dramatically different” from one another. Earlier this summer, Hank Green angered fans when he acknowledged that he had been relying on AI to do research for his videos. (Some observers diagnosed Green’s problem as not one specifically about AI, but rather about overwork and burnout in the creator industry.) It’s not just Green who’s had to defend himself: There are countless stories of brands using or promoting AI — or simply being suspected of doing so — that have spiraled into scandal. For many content creators or public figures, using AI in their work is a reputational risk; is using YouTube’s behind-the-scenes AI tools something they’re worried about? Hanif differentiates between instances where creators are using AI to be more efficient, versus when the tools are doing the actual job of a creator. “What I’ve heard from creators and what I’ve seen from my own conversations with viewers is that when it feels like it’s not actually from the creator, but the tools have taken over and the tools are producing the content, I think that’s kind of where it crosses the line a bit,” Hanif says. Writing the script, shooting the scenes, wholesale creating the content — these are the types of AI use that might become a problem for creators and viewers, he says. The real question is what tangible effects this suite of AI tools actually has on creator success. Does using the chatbot to plan or tweak content help creators connect more with what their audiences want to see? I asked YouTube and Hanif if they had data that shows the tools actually improving metrics for the creators who use them, but the company declined to share anything. “The time that we’ve saved there is time that goes back into the creativity,” Hanif says.

“What I’ve heard from creators and what I’ve seen from my own conversations with viewers is that when it feels like it’s not actually from the creator, but the tools have taken over and the tools are producing the content, I think that’s kind of where it crosses the line a bit,” Hanif says.
Writing the script, shooting the scenes, wholesale creating the content — these are the types of AI use that might become a problem for creators and viewers, he says.
The real question is what tangible effects this suite of AI tools actually has on creator success.
Does using the chatbot to plan or tweak content help creators connect more with what their audiences want to see?
I asked YouTube and Hanif if they had data that shows the tools actually improving metrics for the creators who use them, but the company declined to share anything.
“The time that we’ve saved there is time that goes back into the creativity,” Hanif says.

extraction.body: YouTube is continuing its push into artificial intelligence, unveiling a series of new AI-powered features that aim to simplify video creation, improve content discovery, and help creators grow their audiences. The announcements, highlighted during Google I/O and outlined by YouTube CEO Neal Mohan, signal that AI will remain a major focus for the platform throughout 2026. The latest updates are designed to assist creators at nearly every stage of the production process—from finding ideas and editing videos to reaching viewers in multiple languages. One of the biggest announcements is a new AI-powered conversational search experience called Ask YouTube . Instead of relying solely on keywords, viewers can ask questions in natural language to discover videos related to a specific topic. The feature uses Google’s Gemini AI technology to help users find content more efficiently and receive recommendations that better match their interests. For creators, this could mean optimizing videos around complete questions and helpful answers rather than focusing only on traditional SEO keywords. YouTube is also expanding AI-assisted creative tools that help reduce production time. The goal is to reduce repetitive production tasks while allowing creators to focus on storytelling and audience engagement. Short-form video remains one of YouTube’s fastest-growing formats, and the company continues investing heavily in Shorts. New AI features make it easier for creators to remix content, experiment with new creative formats, and produce engaging vertical videos using Google’s latest generative AI technologies. Google says these tools are intended to lower the barrier for new creators while giving experienced producers additional creative options. In his annual letter outlining the company’s priorities, YouTube CEO Neal Mohan said creators are increasingly building media companies around the platform and that YouTube intends to support them with continued investments in AI, television viewing experiences, creator tools, and business opportunities. The company says AI should help creators work more efficiently rather than replace human creativity. The new AI tools could also benefit businesses using YouTube as part of their marketing strategy. Local businesses can produce educational videos, product demonstrations, customer testimonials, and behind-the-scenes content with fewer technical barriers than in previous years. Companies that consistently publish helpful videos may also benefit as YouTube’s AI improves search and content recommendations based on viewer intent and engagement rather than simple keyword matching. The latest announcements come as competition among video platforms continues to intensify. YouTube recently introduced additional updates to Shorts—including a cleaner viewing mode, 2x playback controls, and interface changes that bring the experience closer to other popular short-video platforms. Industry analysts expect YouTube to continue expanding its AI capabilities throughout the year as Google integrates Gemini technology across more of its products and services. Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how online video is created and consumed. With conversational search, AI-assisted editing, multilingual tools, and generative features becoming more widely available, YouTube is positioning itself to make video production faster and more accessible for creators of every size. Whether the goal is building a personal channel or promoting a local business, YouTube’s newest AI tools could make it easier to reach audiences in an increasingly competitive digital landscape. sources.title: 83% of Gen Z are content creators? Here's where India’s new creator class is coming from
passages: There is a subtle revolution unfolding across India’s digital landscape and it is not led by corporations or legacy media but by Gen Z, the 18–24-year-olds who are rewriting what it means to “make content.” According to a 2024 YouTube India–SmithGeiger report, a staggering 83% of Indian Gen Zers consider themselves creators.
Gen Z in India is treating content creation as real work.
Over 90% of Gen Z creators in the report use YouTube to express their ideas, talents or knowledge.

The implications are huge:A more democratic creator economyA renaissance of regional contentYouth entrepreneurship powered by passion, not just pay checksDigital spaces as platforms for social changeIn the end: The creator dream is realThe next time you scroll through YouTube or watch a video in your local language, remember that the person behind that content is likely part of this Gen Z surge.

It is a profound shift in identity, ambition and how young Indians are forging their futures, especially in cities beyond the megacities.From tier-2 dreams to digital stardomOne of the most striking revelations of the report is about where many of these creators are coming from.
From folk music to regional fashion, they are turning corners of India into digital landmarks.The weight of responsibilityWith power comes responsibility.
In many ways, social media has flattened the opportunity.Creator is the new career: Making money, making meaningThis is not just hobby content anymore.
More than half of the creators surveyed (55%) said digital platforms helped them gain financial independence.

Shorts have been especially pivotal - quick, mobile-first and deeply rooted in the language and styles of smaller-town India.Women are rising in the creator equationThe digital wave is lifting more than just location-diverse creators as it is also lifting the voices of young women.
According to the report, the number of female creators on YouTube has risen by 40% in just the past two years.

The creator economy is no longer side hustle, it is the main hustle and for a generation that grew up online, that feels both natural and powerful.YouTube is their Canvas and their stageWhen it comes to platform choice, YouTube still dominates.
Platforms like YouTube, Instagram and Shorts are not just for fun, they are tools to build businesses, earn sponsorships and monetise passionately.

extraction.body: There is a subtle revolution unfolding across India’s digital landscape and it is not led by corporations or legacy media but by Gen Z, the 18–24-year-olds who are rewriting what it means to “make content.” According to a 2024 YouTube India–SmithGeiger report, a staggering 83% of Indian Gen Zers consider themselves creators. It is a profound shift in identity, ambition and how young Indians are forging their futures, especially in cities beyond the megacities.From tier-2 dreams to digital stardomOne of the most striking revelations of the report is about where many of these creators are coming from. Rather than being concentrated in metros like Mumbai or Delhi, a majority hail from Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, which includes places like Indore, Jaipur, Nagpur and Patna. This matters because for a long time, digital creation was viewed as a ‘big city’ game but now, with a smartphone and Internet, geography has shrunk. In many ways, social media has flattened the opportunity.Creator is the new career: Making money, making meaningThis is not just hobby content anymore. Gen Z in India is treating content creation as real work. According to the report, around 75% of these young creators see content as a genuine career path. Platforms like YouTube, Instagram and Shorts are not just for fun, they are tools to build businesses, earn sponsorships and monetise passionately. story.title: YouTube is building AI creator tools that do almost everything for them

facts.text: At the annual creator-focused Made on YouTube event, the company announced updates to the suite of AI-powered creator tools it unveiled in 2025.
I asked YouTube and Hanif if they had data that shows the tools actually improving metrics for the creators who use them, but the company declined to share anything.
Perhaps most significantly, YouTube is introducing an AI “agent” that will work in the background to optimize a creator’s channel.
Cracking — or fighting — the algorithm has historically been a frustration for creators, but YouTube is increasingly simply telling creators what they should do.

YouTube is taking it a step further, too, by allowing creators to test three different versions of videos — a clip with a different intro and hook, for example, or with a different structure — to see how each performs.
For many content creators or public figures, using AI in their work is a reputational risk; is using YouTube’s behind-the-scenes AI tools something they’re worried about?
In its initial iteration, the dashboard of creator tools included things like A/B testing for video thumbnails and a chatbot interface to query how content was performing.
Hanif says the YouTube system ensures the three video versions are not “dramatically different” from one another.
Hanif differentiates between instances where creators are using AI to be more efficient, versus when the tools are doing the actual job of a creator.

YouTube is continuing its push into artificial intelligence, unveiling a series of new AI-powered features that aim to simplify video creation, improve content discovery, and help creators grow their audiences.
The announcements, highlighted during Google I/O and outlined by YouTube CEO Neal Mohan, signal that AI will remain a major focus for the platform throughout 2026.
New AI features make it easier for creators to remix content, experiment with new creative formats, and produce engaging vertical videos using Google’s latest generative AI technologies.
Google says these tools are intended to lower the barrier for new creators while giving experienced producers additional creative options.
YouTube is also expanding AI-assisted creative tools that help reduce production time.
The new AI tools could also benefit businesses using YouTube as part of their marketing strategy.

Companies that consistently publish helpful videos may also benefit as YouTube’s AI improves search and content recommendations based on viewer intent and engagement rather than simple keyword matching.
Local businesses can produce educational videos, product demonstrations, customer testimonials, and behind-the-scenes content with fewer technical barriers than in previous years.
Industry analysts expect YouTube to continue expanding its AI capabilities throughout the year as Google integrates Gemini technology across more of its products and services.
Creators around the world in our YouTube Shorts Creator Community are pioneering new ways to use generative AI to simplify their content strategy and explore new creative boundaries.
I use an AI program to cut down long-form content into snappy and relevant short-form videos.
They specialize in entertainment content focused on funny Shorts, family challenges, tests, and experiments.
Arman is an Indonesian content creator who combines music and entertainment on his Shorts.
He considers himself one of the “OG” creators who has been creating content for 8+ years on YouTube.
Even though we are satisfied with the tools and data from YouTube Studio, we can maximize it again with AI to take the next steps, and can even speed up solutions in content creation.
AI is a sophisticated tool that can make creators' work easier, saving us time, money and energy in creating quality content.
Explore the latest company news, creator and artist profiles, culture and trends analyses, and behind-the-scenes insights on the YouTube Official Blog.
From helping create a multi-format strategy to developing new series on Shorts, AI is top of mind for many creators from the US to Brazil, Turkey, Indonesia, and beyond.
As a content creator and digital content expert, I can develop more creative and innovative projects by saving time and resources thanks to artificial intelligence applications and tools.

extraction.body: Washington DC: The Donald Trump administration on Tuesday defended its decision to bar journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The Justice Department said that the media houses can be barred from the White House at the US President’s will. The department, in a court filing, argued that “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," reported CNN. The filing further contended that Trump has the authority to restrict access to private sections of the White House to safeguard sensitive national security information. “At the very least, the Government may control reporters’ access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office, even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons,” the Justice Department wrote in its filing, as reported by CNN. “The President has found that Plaintiffs have engaged in a number of reporting incidents that have threatened national security. Such reporting directly raises national security concerns,” it added. The Justice Department’s court filing came a day ahead of an emergency hearing before federal judge Timothy Kelly in Washington, DC. The petitioners, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, are demanding for the immediate restoration of their media access. Reasons For Banning These Media Outlets: The latest court filings also include letters sent to the three media organisations on Tuesday, outlining the reasons cited by the President for imposing the access ban. These letters cite several stories published by the banned media outlets. The letter addressed to CNN referred to the network’s report about Trump’s plans for a “top secret” bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom under construction, along with several of its reports on the Iran war. The letter to MS NOW slammed the media house for its coverage of the Iran war. As per a CNN report citing these letters, Politico’s entry was banned due to its reporting on Iran, the ballroom and Russia sanctions. About The Dispute: The dispute began last week when Trump barred journalists from the three outlets from entering the White House grounds. CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to restore their access, arguing that the restrictions violate their First Amendment rights. At the same time, ABC, CBS, Fox News, and NBC suspended their pooled television coverage of Trump after the White House prevented CNN from carrying out its scheduled role as pool representative during his trip to the United Nations General Assembly. Trump's Clarification: Trump strongly defended the decision in multiple Truth Social posts, rejecting the allegations that the White House was attacking the free press. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” Trump wrote. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.” He described the coverage from the three outlets as “corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” and said it was “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Trump also argued that the media organizations should not automatically receive access to the White House.

This includes the article content, images, author information, and related articles. The Justice Department has urged a federal court to uphold President Trump's ban on CNN, MSNOW, and Politico, arguing White House access is not a public right. The United States Department of Justice has formally defended President Donald Trump's decision to ban three major news organizations from the White House, arguing in a late-night court filing that presidential access is a "privilege—not a right." The legal maneuver seeks to uphold the administration's revocation of press credentials for journalists from CNN, MSNOW, and Politico, citing severe national security concerns and alleged breaches of professional decorum. The filing, submitted to a federal court in Washington, D.C. on Tuesday evening, arrived just hours before an emergency hearing concerning the media outlets' request for a temporary restraining order. The news organizations are suing the Trump administration to immediately restore their White House access, characterizing the ban as a flagrant violation of their First Amendment rights. The escalating legal battle underscores the highly adversarial relationship between the White House and the press corps during Trump's presidency, raising fundamental questions about the government's authority to control public information and exclude critical voices from the seat of executive power. In its submission to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, the Justice Department argued that the First Amendment does not grant journalists an unrestrained, independent right to access highly controlled government facilities. The DOJ maintained that the president possesses broad, discretionary authority to manage entry to restricted areas, including the Oval Office. "The White House is the home and workplace for the Nation's Commander-in-Chief," DOJ Attorney Michael Velchik wrote in the filing. "But the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by publishing sensitive or classified information." The government asserted that it holds a compelling interest in enforcing these minimum standards and safeguarding classified material. The DOJ further claimed that the administration is legally permitted to control reporters' access to restricted presidential areas "even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons," a stark legal position that challenges established norms of press freedom. The DOJ's filing included copies of formal letters sent by the White House Press Office to the three networks on Tuesday, outlining the administration's specific grievances. The letters accused the outlets of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security" and cited a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents that the White House deemed dangerous. For CNN, the administration flagged January reports detailing the construction of a top-secret bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom, alongside coverage concerning US military munitions shortages amid the ongoing conflict with Iran. MSNOW was criticized for its reporting on the Iran war and its coverage of internal White House leak investigations. Politico faced similar accusations regarding its articles on Russian sanctions and the diplomatic fallout from the Middle East conflict. The letters provided the news organizations with a strict deadline of 5:00 p.m. on Friday, September 25, to formally contest the initial decision, warning that failure to respond would render the revocations permanent. The media outlets have strongly denied that their reporting compromised national security. extraction.body: Washington — Justice Department lawyers on Tuesday defended President Trump's move to bar three news outlets from the White House over coverage of his administration, arguing that their reporting raises national security concerns and claiming their journalists failed to act with "professionalism and decorum."In a filing with a federal district court in Washington, D.C., the Trump administration argued the president's ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico is legally sound. Reporters from those news organizations were stripped of their press credentials, also called "hard passes," denying them access to the White House grounds."Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," Justice Department lawyers wrote.The Trump administration argued the president's ban complies with the First Amendment, because the government has at least two "compelling reasons" for denying the reporters' access: enforcing "minimum standards of professionalism" for the press and protecting classified information."The President believes basic journalistic standards require calling, asking for comment, and providing a reasonable opportunity for a response," they said. "At a bare minimum, it is a significant violation of decorum to publish classified and sensitive national security information."The Justice Department also submitted to the court letters from the White House press office, dated Tuesday, to each of the three outlets notifying them that the president decided to revoke their journalists' hard passes. The letters claim that the news outlets have "exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."The White House gave CNN, MS NOW and Politico a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to respond to its claims.The letters appear designed to address the news outlets' claims that the ban deprived them of due process, since their reporters didn't receive advance notice that they would be denied access to the White House and an opportunity to be heard before revoking their credentials."The President provided no notice that he would immediately deny news organizations whose reporting he dislikes access to the White House grounds," lawyers for the organizations said in a filing. "His standard for denying access is arbitrary and vague — indeed, it can hardly be called a standard at all."The Justice Department's response comes ahead of a hearing, set for Wednesday afternoon, during which a judge will consider whether to order the White House to restore the media organizations' credentials and access. CBS News and dozens of other news organizations have signed onto an amicus brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.The three news organizations sued Mr. Trump and top administration officials on Monday, calling his ban a "direct assault on the First Amendment" and a "blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles." The lawsuit names Mr. Trump and three of his top aides: Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff; Steven Cheung, White House communications director; and Sean Curran, the head of Secret Service. Trump during his first term, to rule quickly to once again allow them access to the White House. The organizations argued in their court filings that the ban violates their due process rights because Mr. Trump "provided no notice" to the companies before banning them, and no opportunity for CNN, MS NOW, or Politico to oppose the ban before it was announced and reporters for the news outlets had their press credentials confiscated.The ban, the organizations say, also violates the First Amendment because it "brazenly discriminates based on editorial viewpoint," and "to coerce more favorable coverage of the administration from CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, and to deter other journalists and news organizations from reporting that the President might view as unfavorable."Kelly oversaw a lawsuit brought by former CNN reporter Jim Acosta during the first Trump administration after the White House moved to revoke his press credential. The judge sided with Acosta after CNN sued and ordered his press pass to be restored, finding Acosta's due process rights under the Fifth Amendment had been violated. The White House complied with the order, and CNN dropped the lawsuit shortly afterward.Mr. Trump has also barred The Associated Press from attending certain White House events after the news outlet refused to conform to Mr. Trump's proclamation that changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to "Gulf of America." The wire service sued on First Amendment grounds. While a federal judge in D.C. initially ruled that the White House must restore the news outlet's access, an appeals court later allowed the ban to take effect. The litigation in that case is ongoing.The ruling from the U.S. Circuit hinged on the fact that the AP was blocked from certain restricted spaces like the Oval Office and Air Force One that only a small subset of the White House press corps can access — a narrower policy than the outright ban imposed on CNN, MS NOW and Politico. In a 2-1 decision, the two judges in the majority, Neomi Rao and Gregory Katsas, said the White House can't ban journalists from spaces that are "generally open to the press," like the briefing room, based on their viewpoint. Trump appointed both Rao and Katsas to the D.C. Trump returned to the White House for his second term, his press office assumed control of the press pool, a rotating group of journalists who cover the president every day and disseminate information and footage to thousands of other news outlets. The president's ban has already disrupted that information flow: CNN is a member of the television pool system, which includes CBS News, ABC News, NBC News and Fox News, and was scheduled to travel with Mr. Trump to New York on Monday for the United Nations General Assembly.But the network, which was set to provide coverage in the TV pool slot, was kicked off the trip because of the president's ban. As a result, the four other networks in the rotation decided to suspend the television pool altogether in solidarity with their CNN colleagues.

extraction.body: Washington DC: The Donald Trump administration on Tuesday defended its decision to bar journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The Justice Department said that the media houses can be barred from the White House at the US President’s will. The department, in a court filing, argued that “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," reported CNN. The filing further contended that Trump has the authority to restrict access to private sections of the White House to safeguard sensitive national security information. “At the very least, the Government may control reporters’ access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office, even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons,” the Justice Department wrote in its filing, as reported by CNN. “The President has found that Plaintiffs have engaged in a number of reporting incidents that have threatened national security. Such reporting directly raises national security concerns,” it added. The Justice Department’s court filing came a day ahead of an emergency hearing before federal judge Timothy Kelly in Washington, DC. The petitioners, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, are demanding for the immediate restoration of their media access. Reasons For Banning These Media Outlets: The latest court filings also include letters sent to the three media organisations on Tuesday, outlining the reasons cited by the President for imposing the access ban. These letters cite several stories published by the banned media outlets. The letter addressed to CNN referred to the network’s report about Trump’s plans for a “top secret” bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom under construction, along with several of its reports on the Iran war. The letter to MS NOW slammed the media house for its coverage of the Iran war. As per a CNN report citing these letters, Politico’s entry was banned due to its reporting on Iran, the ballroom and Russia sanctions. About The Dispute: The dispute began last week when Trump barred journalists from the three outlets from entering the White House grounds. CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to restore their access, arguing that the restrictions violate their First Amendment rights. At the same time, ABC, CBS, Fox News, and NBC suspended their pooled television coverage of Trump after the White House prevented CNN from carrying out its scheduled role as pool representative during his trip to the United Nations General Assembly. Trump's Clarification: Trump strongly defended the decision in multiple Truth Social posts, rejecting the allegations that the White House was attacking the free press. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” Trump wrote. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.” He described the coverage from the three outlets as “corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” and said it was “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Trump also argued that the media organizations should not automatically receive access to the White House.

The Justice Department has urged a federal court to uphold President Trump's ban on CNN, MSNOW, and Politico, arguing White House access is not a public right. The United States Department of Justice has formally defended President Donald Trump's decision to ban three major news organizations from the White House, arguing in a late-night court filing that presidential access is a "privilege—not a right." The legal maneuver seeks to uphold the administration's revocation of press credentials for journalists from CNN, MSNOW, and Politico, citing severe national security concerns and alleged breaches of professional decorum. The filing, submitted to a federal court in Washington, D.C. on Tuesday evening, arrived just hours before an emergency hearing concerning the media outlets' request for a temporary restraining order. The news organizations are suing the Trump administration to immediately restore their White House access, characterizing the ban as a flagrant violation of their First Amendment rights. The escalating legal battle underscores the highly adversarial relationship between the White House and the press corps during Trump's presidency, raising fundamental questions about the government's authority to control public information and exclude critical voices from the seat of executive power. In its submission to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, the Justice Department argued that the First Amendment does not grant journalists an unrestrained, independent right to access highly controlled government facilities. The DOJ maintained that the president possesses broad, discretionary authority to manage entry to restricted areas, including the Oval Office. "The White House is the home and workplace for the Nation's Commander-in-Chief," DOJ Attorney Michael Velchik wrote in the filing. "But the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by publishing sensitive or classified information." The government asserted that it holds a compelling interest in enforcing these minimum standards and safeguarding classified material. The DOJ further claimed that the administration is legally permitted to control reporters' access to restricted presidential areas "even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons," a stark legal position that challenges established norms of press freedom. The DOJ's filing included copies of formal letters sent by the White House Press Office to the three networks on Tuesday, outlining the administration's specific grievances. The letters accused the outlets of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security" and cited a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents that the White House deemed dangerous. For CNN, the administration flagged January reports detailing the construction of a top-secret bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom, alongside coverage concerning US military munitions shortages amid the ongoing conflict with Iran. MSNOW was criticized for its reporting on the Iran war and its coverage of internal White House leak investigations. Politico faced similar accusations regarding its articles on Russian sanctions and the diplomatic fallout from the Middle East conflict. The letters provided the news organizations with a strict deadline of 5:00 p.m. on Friday, September 25, to formally contest the initial decision, warning that failure to respond would render the revocations permanent. The media outlets have strongly denied that their reporting compromised national security. Legal representatives for the networks argue that the cited articles relied on corroborated sources and standard journalistic practices, portraying the administration's national security claims as a pretext for punishing unfavorable coverage. The current controversy erupted on Friday when Trump announced the bans via a post on his Truth Social platform, declaring the move "effective immediately." He justified the decision by accusing the networks of reporting "fiction and lies" and suggested that other media organizations might face similar expulsions. Press freedom advocates have condemned the bans as a retaliatory tactic designed to chill independent journalism. Legal experts note that federal courts have historically sided with the press when the Trump administration previously attempted to revoke individual credentials, such as the high-profile disputes involving CNN's Jim Acosta and Brian Karem during his first term. In those instances, courts ruled that the administration could not arbitrarily revoke credentials without providing rigorous due process. However, the Justice Department is now attempting to establish a broader legal precedent, leaning heavily on the argument that the physical security of the White House supersedes general press access rights. The government explicitly argued that the bans were not retaliatory, claiming that the administration would have taken the same action regarding the classified leaks regardless of the outlets' broader editorial criticism of the president. The outcome of Wednesday's emergency hearing will carry significant implications for the functioning of the White House press corps. Without a traveling pool representative from CNN, the television network pool was left empty during the president's movements earlier in the week, disrupting the standard distribution of presidential activities to the broader public. As the legal proceedings advance, the confrontation highlights a critical constitutional tension. While the government insists on its right to control the physical perimeter of the executive branch, media organizations warn that allowing a president to unilaterally ban specific outlets based on their reporting fundamentally undermines the democratic principle of a free and unhindered press. The escalating legal battle underscores the highly adversarial relationship between the White House and the press corps during Trump's presidency, raising fundamental questions about the government's authority to control public information and exclude critical voices from the seat of executive power.

In its submission to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, the Justice Department argued that the First Amendment does not grant journalists an unrestrained, independent right to access highly controlled government facilities. The DOJ maintained that the president possesses broad, discretionary authority to manage entry to restricted areas, including the Oval Office.

"The White House is the home and workplace for the Nation's Commander-in-Chief," DOJ Attorney Michael Velchik wrote in the filing. "But the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by publishing sensitive or classified information."

The government asserted that it holds a compelling interest in enforcing these minimum standards and safeguarding classified material. The DOJ further claimed that the administration is legally permitted to control reporters' access to restricted presidential areas "even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons," a stark legal position that challenges established norms of press freedom.

The DOJ's filing included copies of formal letters sent by the White House Press Office to the three networks on Tuesday, outlining the administration's specific grievances. The letters accused the outlets of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security" and cited a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents that the White House deemed dangerous.

For CNN, the administration flagged January reports detailing the construction of a top-secret bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom, alongside coverage concerning US military munitions shortages amid the ongoing conflict with Iran. MSNOW was criticized for its reporting on the Iran war and its coverage of internal White House leak investigations. Politico faced similar accusations regarding its articles on Russian sanctions and the diplomatic fallout from the Middle East conflict.

The letters provided the news organizations with a strict deadline of 5:00 p.m. on Friday, September 25, to formally contest the initial decision, warning that failure to respond would render the revocations permanent.

The media outlets have strongly denied that their reporting compromised national security. Legal representatives for the networks argue that the cited articles relied on corroborated sources and standard journalistic practices, portraying the administration's national security claims as a pretext for punishing unfavorable coverage.

The current controversy erupted on Friday when Trump announced the bans via a post on his Truth Social platform, declaring the move "effective immediately." He justified the decision by accusing the networks of reporting "fiction and lies" and suggested that other media organizations might face similar expulsions.

Press freedom advocates have condemned the bans as a retaliatory tactic designed to chill independent journalism. Legal experts note that federal courts have historically sided with the press when the Trump administration previously attempted to revoke individual credentials, such as the high-profile disputes involving CNN's Jim Acosta and Brian Karem during his first term. In those instances, courts ruled that the administration could not arbitrarily revoke credentials without providing rigorous due process.

However, the Justice Department is now attempting to establish a broader legal precedent, leaning heavily on the argument that the physical security of the White House supersedes general press access rights. The government explicitly argued that the bans were not retaliatory, claiming that the administration would have taken the same action regarding the classified leaks regardless of the outlets' broader editorial criticism of the president.

The outcome of Wednesday's emergency hearing will carry significant implications for the functioning of the White House press corps. Without a traveling pool representative from CNN, the television network pool was left empty during the president's movements earlier in the week, disrupting the standard distribution of presidential activities to the broader public.

As the legal proceedings advance, the confrontation highlights a critical constitutional tension. While the government insists on its right to control the physical perimeter of the executive branch, media organizations warn that allowing a president to unilaterally ban specific outlets based on their reporting fundamentally undermines the democratic principle of a free and unhindered press.

extraction.body: Washington — Justice Department lawyers on Tuesday defended President Trump's move to bar three news outlets from the White House over coverage of his administration, arguing that their reporting raises national security concerns and claiming their journalists failed to act with "professionalism and decorum."In a filing with a federal district court in Washington, D.C., the Trump administration argued the president's ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico is legally sound. Reporters from those news organizations were stripped of their press credentials, also called "hard passes," denying them access to the White House grounds."Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," Justice Department lawyers wrote.The Trump administration argued the president's ban complies with the First Amendment, because the government has at least two "compelling reasons" for denying the reporters' access: enforcing "minimum standards of professionalism" for the press and protecting classified information."The President believes basic journalistic standards require calling, asking for comment, and providing a reasonable opportunity for a response," they said. "At a bare minimum, it is a significant violation of decorum to publish classified and sensitive national security information."The Justice Department also submitted to the court letters from the White House press office, dated Tuesday, to each of the three outlets notifying them that the president decided to revoke their journalists' hard passes. The letters claim that the news outlets have "exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."The White House gave CNN, MS NOW and Politico a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to respond to its claims.The letters appear designed to address the news outlets' claims that the ban deprived them of due process, since their reporters didn't receive advance notice that they would be denied access to the White House and an opportunity to be heard before revoking their credentials."The President provided no notice that he would immediately deny news organizations whose reporting he dislikes access to the White House grounds," lawyers for the organizations said in a filing. "His standard for denying access is arbitrary and vague — indeed, it can hardly be called a standard at all."The Justice Department's response comes ahead of a hearing, set for Wednesday afternoon, during which a judge will consider whether to order the White House to restore the media organizations' credentials and access. CBS News and dozens of other news organizations have signed onto an amicus brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.The three news organizations sued Mr. Trump and top administration officials on Monday, calling his ban a "direct assault on the First Amendment" and a "blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles." The lawsuit names Mr. Trump and three of his top aides: Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff; Steven Cheung, White House communications director; and Sean Curran, the head of Secret Service. Trump during his first term, to rule quickly to once again allow them access to the White House. The organizations argued in their court filings that the ban violates their due process rights because Mr. Trump "provided no notice" to the companies before banning them, and no opportunity for CNN, MS NOW, or Politico to oppose the ban before it was announced and reporters for the news outlets had their press credentials confiscated.The ban, the organizations say, also violates the First Amendment because it "brazenly discriminates based on editorial viewpoint," and "to coerce more favorable coverage of the administration from CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, and to deter other journalists and news organizations from reporting that the President might view as unfavorable."Kelly oversaw a lawsuit brought by former CNN reporter Jim Acosta during the first Trump administration after the White House moved to revoke his press credential. The judge sided with Acosta after CNN sued and ordered his press pass to be restored, finding Acosta's due process rights under the Fifth Amendment had been violated. The White House complied with the order, and CNN dropped the lawsuit shortly afterward.Mr. Trump has also barred The Associated Press from attending certain White House events after the news outlet refused to conform to Mr. Trump's proclamation that changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to "Gulf of America." The wire service sued on First Amendment grounds. While a federal judge in D.C. initially ruled that the White House must restore the news outlet's access, an appeals court later allowed the ban to take effect. The litigation in that case is ongoing.The ruling from the U.S. Circuit hinged on the fact that the AP was blocked from certain restricted spaces like the Oval Office and Air Force One that only a small subset of the White House press corps can access — a narrower policy than the outright ban imposed on CNN, MS NOW and Politico. In a 2-1 decision, the two judges in the majority, Neomi Rao and Gregory Katsas, said the White House can't ban journalists from spaces that are "generally open to the press," like the briefing room, based on their viewpoint. Trump appointed both Rao and Katsas to the D.C. Trump returned to the White House for his second term, his press office assumed control of the press pool, a rotating group of journalists who cover the president every day and disseminate information and footage to thousands of other news outlets. The president's ban has already disrupted that information flow: CNN is a member of the television pool system, which includes CBS News, ABC News, NBC News and Fox News, and was scheduled to travel with Mr. Trump to New York on Monday for the United Nations General Assembly.But the network, which was set to provide coverage in the TV pool slot, was kicked off the trip because of the president's ban. As a result, the four other networks in the rotation decided to suspend the television pool altogether in solidarity with their CNN colleagues.

The DOJ argues that such access is a “privilege” that news agencies enjoy, and states that presidents have the legal authority to block whoever they want. “Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the DOJ filing forcefully claims , adding that Trump can enforce “minimum standards for bona fide journalists and safeguarding national security information.” The filing also argues that these news orgs were unprofessional through their use of anonymous sources to publish stories about the White House — a practice that has existed for decades, if not longer, and which Trump himself has utilized in the past to criticize his political opponents. Attempting to prove Trump’s order should remain in place, the filing cites CNN’s reporting on a bunker underneath Trump’s planned East Wing ballroom; MS NOW’s reporting on the White House’s investigation into leaks; and Politico’s reporting on Secret Service funds being used to help pay for security improvements in the planned ballroom. It is unclear how the outlets’ reporting on these subjects detrimentally affects national security — indeed, the reports contain information that the American public may have a vested interest in. A court hearing in the case is set for Wednesday, Sept. 23, before U.S. District Court Judge Timothy Kelly. "At a bare minimum, it is a significant violation of decorum to publish classified and sensitive national security information," it continues. The government's attorneys – representing Trump and other White House officials listed as co-defendants – asked the judge to deny the three media outlets' request for an injunction to halt Trump's ban. The Justice Department's response to the lawsuit highlights multiple stories from the three outlets based on anonymous sourcing that the government alleges "threatened national security." The examples, detailed in letters to each publication on Tuesday, include stories on national security elements planned for Trump's White House ballroom, information about the Iran war and U.S. munitions stockpiles. "Plaintiffs’ reporting gives rise to reasons to doubt their trustworthiness and, in fact, the President has determined that Plaintiffs have reported classified or sensitive information bearing on national security," the government's motion reads. "Defendants have a compelling governmental interest in protecting such information." Attorneys single out a Politico report, for example, that painted Trump's recent Republican midterm convention in Dallas as a "disaster," arguing that the convention's strong livestream viewership proves it wasn't. On Sept. 19, the day after Trump announced his ban, reporters for CNN, MS NOW and Politico were blocked by security from entering the White House, and their White House press passes were confiscated. Knight case, when a federal appeals court ruled that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny press passes to reporters based on the content of their coverage if the White House has voluntarily opened its doors to media and established facilities for the press.

MSFT shares traded marginally in the green at the time of writing. Microsoft Plans $10B-Plus Regional Investment The company plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the Middle East between now and 2030 as it expands cloud and AI infrastructure, increases capacity and introduces new capabilities. Microsoft also said it will deepen relationships with governments and national AI organizations, citing partnerships with HUMAIN, G42, QAI and the Government of Kuwait. Alongside its cloud and AI expansion, Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030. Microsoft cited its existing participation in subsea cable systems including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the U.A.E., as well as its global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. The company also plans to strengthen cybersecurity cooperation with authorities in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the U.A.E. through dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions. Separately, Microsoft said it will expand AI governance work and collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation (RAIFF), which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI). On the workforce side, Microsoft said it will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, and talent development across the four countries. The company said this builds on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030, including through programs targeting public-sector leaders, students, workers and women. extraction.body: Microsoft on September 23, 2026, announced a new framework for the Middle East focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, saying it plans to invest more than $10 billion in the region through 2030 across technology, digital resilience, and people initiatives. The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, naming HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. It pointed to digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. The partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield where relevant and available. The company also plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. Microsoft said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and that it operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft said, it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, and will work with governments and local stakeholders on water stewardship across the region. It also said it will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative offering digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The announcement states that conflict in the region has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. The company said it will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. Those commitments will be complemented by Microsoft’s sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience. Microsoft also announced it is deepening partnerships with cybersecurity authorities in the four countries. A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate those resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across the company. On responsible AI, Microsoft said it will work to strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region, support practical approaches to testing, evaluation, and assurance systems, and expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence , on responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue research and partnerships in the region focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the framework’s people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across the four countries, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions, building on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, the AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the region to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy and helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning. It also said it will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. The announcement closes by noting that Microsoft has been part of the region for more than 35 years and stating that the company is committed to remaining a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educators, and communities across the Middle East. passages: Sep 23, 2026 | By Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President of Microsoft

Microsoft has served the Middle East since it began operations in the region in 1991. Since then, we’ve steadily expanded our presence and investments, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations. Today, Microsoft is reaffirming that commitment through a new framework focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.

We are expanding our investments in the Middle East with confidence in the region’s future as it pursues one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations. We will add to our local partnerships across the region. We will build on the work we have done to stand by these countries’ governments and people through a period of significant challenges. As we look to the future, we will invest further in technology, digital resilience, and the people across the region.
From now until 2030, we will pursue the following initiatives with our partners in the region:
We will deepen our partnerships through national AI champions

Microsoft will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations to translate AI ambition into economic growth, modern public services, and global competitiveness. This builds on work with organizations including HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait, alongside digital-government initiatives such as TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait.

These partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses. They will be supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield, where relevant and available.
We will invest in subsea and terrestrial connectivity

Digital resilience depends on strong and reliable networks. Protecting subsea and terrestrial connectivity requires sustained cooperation between governments and the private sector, but the foundation of continuity is redundancy. A diverse network of high-capacity routes allows traffic to be rerouted around disruptions, minimizing latency and maintaining critical data flows.

Microsoft has helped expand both the capacity and reliability of digital connectivity across regions through investments in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, as well as operating a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft has demonstrated the value of redundancy by rerouting traffic through Middle East corridors and maintaining service continuity with minimal impact on customers.

Building on this foundation, Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030. This investment will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support Microsoft’s growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint across the region.
We will build AI infrastructure with the planet in mind

As we expand our cloud and AI infrastructure in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will do so with a focus on responsible growth. Guided by Microsoft’s global goals to address carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems, we will work with our lessor partners to ensure that the cloud infrastructure supporting our services advances Microsoft’s water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible.

Water resilience is particularly important across the Middle East. Building on Microsoft’s global experience advancing water stewardship through water reuse, replenishment, and innovative water management solutions, we will work with governments and local stakeholders to identify opportunities that advance responsible water stewardship across the region.

As AI accelerates economic opportunity across the Middle East, expanding access to clean energy will be essential to ensuring this growth is sustainable. We will also collaborate with regulators, utilities, and our lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. By combining infrastructure investment with local partnerships and innovation, we aim to support the region’s energy and water priorities while helping build the sustainable foundations needed for long-term AI-led economic growth.
We will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative

Conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. Microsoft has worked with customers to support business continuity through resilience options tailored to different operational and regulatory needs. Going forward, Microsoft will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy, helping organizations strengthen continuity and recovery through digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities.
We will strengthen data protection, privacy, and business continuity

Microsoft will expand our existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. These are designed to give organizations greater confidence in how their data, systems, and operations are protected while maintaining continuity in times of uncertainty. They will be complemented by Microsoft’s growing sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience.
We will expand and strengthen cybersecurity cooperation

As Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE accelerate their digital transformation, cybersecurity has become a core pillar of national and economic security. As governments, critical infrastructure, and economies become more connected, cyber threats and influence operations can have consequences that extend far beyond physical borders. That’s why we are announcing that we are deepening our partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in these countries.

A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate these resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft. Stronger cybersecurity benefits far more than individual networks. It helps build trust to ensure digital transformation will succeed.
We will advance responsible AI through governance, assurance, and inclusion

Microsoft will work with governments, businesses, researchers, and civil society organizations across the Middle East to help people and institutions benefit from new technology. As AI advances, realizing its full potential will require not only access to powerful technology, but the governance, assurance, and skills required to deploy it confidently and responsibly.

We will help strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region and support practical approaches to testing, evaluating, and assurance systems. We will also expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation (RAIFF), co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools that can be applied across high-impact AI use cases in the Middle East and beyond.

Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue to support the region through research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience. This includes work through initiatives such as the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities.

In partnership with governments, NGOs, nonprofits, and research institutions, the AI for Good Lab will continue developing and scaling AI solutions that address real-world challenges across the Middle East and beyond.

This includes supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings. Across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will work with local partners to ensure students and educators can benefit from AI safely, responsibly, and effectively and will engage educators, policymakers, industry leaders, and civil society to support practical approaches to AI implementation that reflect local priorities.

The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, naming HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. It pointed to digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. The partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield where relevant and available. The company also plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. Microsoft said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and that it operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft said, it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, and will work with governments and local stakeholders on water stewardship across the region. It also said it will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative offering digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The announcement states that conflict in the region has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. The company said it will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. Those commitments will be complemented by Microsoft’s sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience. Microsoft also announced it is deepening partnerships with cybersecurity authorities in the four countries. A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate those resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across the company. On responsible AI, Microsoft said it will work to strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region, support practical approaches to testing, evaluation, and assurance systems, and expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence , on responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue research and partnerships in the region focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the framework’s people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across the four countries, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions, building on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, the AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the region to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy and helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning. It also said it will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. The announcement closes by noting that Microsoft has been part of the region for more than 35 years and stating that the company is committed to remaining a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educators, and communities across the Middle East. The new framework is focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates and is organized around three areas: technology, digital resilience, and people. Microsoft said it will pursue the initiatives with partners in the region from now until 2030.

Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since it began operations in the region in 1991, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations.

The company said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings.

Microsoft said it will also partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that support national talent strategies and policy recommendations.
